QUESTION: What are the external connection ports on the robot?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot provides several external connection ports on the Control Box underside and at the tool flange/Wrist 3:

- Mini DisplayPort (Control Box underside) — supports DisplayPort; requires an active Mini Display to DVI/HDMI converter (passive adapters do not work). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]

- Ethernet (Control Box underside) — for MODBUS, EtherNet/IP, PROFINET, remote access/control (10–1000 Mb/s). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]

- Tool connector (on Wrist 3 / tool flange) — 8‑pin tool I/O providing power, digital I/O, analog I/O and RS485 signals (pins and functions listed in the manual). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

- General purpose analog I/O (green terminal on Control Box) — 0–10 V or 4–20 mA inputs/outputs. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

- General purpose digital I/O (gray and configurable yellow terminals on Control Box) — 24 V digital inputs/outputs for interfacing with PLCs and equipment. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

- Remote ON/OFF control terminals (Control Box) — auxiliary 12 V supply plus ON/OFF inputs for remotely turning the Control Box on/off. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

Notices/warnings: do not connect or disconnect the Teach Pendant while the Control Box is powered on (can cause damage), and plug in active display adapters before powering the Control Box. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Define Safety Planes and Tool Position limits in the Safety configuration: use safety planes to restrict the tool and/or elbow, and define tool spheres (Tool Position) so the robot enforces those limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Key steps and notes:
- Create and name the required feature(s) (point or plane) in Installation > Features before unlocking the Safety tab; the robot powers off when Safety is unlocked so features must exist first. [010__L1__10._10.4...pdf]
- Add up to eight Safety Planes (Installation > Safety > Planes) and configure each plane’s mode (Disabled / Normal / Reduced / Normal & Reduced / Trigger Reduced). Planes can restrict the Tool and/or Restrict Elbow; disable either checkbox to allow passage. [010__L1__10._10.4...pdf]
- Set Restrict Elbow to prevent the elbow joint (treated as a sphere) from passing the plane; UR5e elbow sphere diameter = 0.13 m. [010__L1__10._10.4...pdf]
- Use Tool Position to define user tools (spheres) with position and radius (0–300 mm). The safety planes treat the tool as a sphere and prevent any point on that sphere from crossing a safety plane. Ensure a Tool Position is set so trigger planes work correctly. [010__L1__10._10.4...pdf]
- Perform an application risk assessment and choose safety limits (Normal/Reduced) appropriate to your application; safety settings must match the assessed risks. [010__L1__10._10.2...pdf][004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If you need exact menu steps or examples, see the Tool Position and Safety Planes procedures in the Safety section. [010__L1__10._10.4...pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Direct answer:
Safety planes limit robot position but you must account for the robot motion after a stop is initiated (stopping distance/time) and avoid creating pinch or other hazards in the workspace [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

Supporting points:
- Safety planes take the expected stopping distance into account (the robot will slow before the plane), so configure Stopping Time Limit / Stopping Distance Limit as part of the risk assessment to ensure the robot stops before the plane is reached [010__L1__10...pdf].  
- Incorrect safety configuration (including speed limits) or failure to set password protection can create hazardous situations or allow unauthorized changes to safety planes—always perform an application risk assessment and secure safety settings [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Be aware of workspace pinch hazards (radial and near-base areas); use safety planes and joint limits to prevent the robot entering pinch zones or remove obstacles from those areas [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the safety system is limiting or stopping motion (Recovery or Reduced mode) because a safety limit is violated or a safety input/state is active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting points:
- If a safety limit is violated at power-on or during operation, the controller starts in Recovery mode where movement is restricted by fixed recovery limits (slower motion) until you move the arm back within limits; joint/plane/orientation limits are disabled in Recovery so manual caution is required. Recovery triggers Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Normal vs Reduced mode: if the robot is on the reduced side of a trigger plane or a reduced input is active, the robot uses more restrictive limits (slower speeds) and can transition with up to 500 ms delay. If this does not explain your case, check the Safety Checksum and Safety Configuration to confirm no unexpected safety settings, verify whether Recovery or Reduced mode is active, and inspect configured safety inputs/trigger planes. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- After any liquid exposure you must visually inspect the robot and the installation, dry affected parts, and verify safety functions and wiring as part of the application risk assessment before powering/operating the robot. QUESTION: How do I lock the X axis from rotating on the arm when in freedrive mode?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use the Freedrive panel and lock rotation for the TCP (or lock the specific axis) in PolyScope.

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes plus tool/elbow restrictions and tool-position spheres.

- Define feature(s) (point or plane) in Installation first, then create safety plane(s) in Safety → Planes. Configure plane Mode (Normal/Reduced/Trigger Reduced) and which side is allowed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable "Restrict Elbow" on a plane to prevent the robot elbow joint sphere from crossing that plane (UR5e elbow sphere radius = 0.13 m). Note the elbow restriction uses a sphere radius defined per robot. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Define Tool Position (Safety → Tool Position): create or copy a TCP, set its Position and Radius (0–300 mm). The safety system treats the tool as a point or sphere; safety planes prevent any point on that sphere from crossing the plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Optionally restrict the Tool Flange to prevent the flange (and attached tool) from crossing a plane; remove flange restriction if you need the flange to cross and only the tool tip to be constrained (useful with large tool offsets). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes/warnings:
- Safety planes only limit the defined Tool spheres and elbow sphere, not the entire robot arm—other parts may not obey the plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Create and name features before unlocking Safety (robot powers off when Safety Tab unlocked). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Configure limits according to your integrator’s risk assessment and apply/save the safety configuration. [010__L1__10._10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Safety planes define spatial limits that can restrict either the tool/end effector alone or both the tool/end effector and the elbow, and are used to reduce risks identified in the application risk assessment [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

- Risks and cautions:
  - Incorrect or missing configuration of safety planes can leave hazards uneliminated or insufficiently reduced — follow the application risk assessment and do not change safety configuration without authorization [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
  - Safety planes take expected stopping distance into account, and stopping-time/distance limits affect robot speed to ensure the robot can stop before the plane is crossed — set stopping limits appropriately in the risk assessment [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
  - If a safety limit is violated or a fault occurs, the safety system may initiate an immediate power-removal stop (Stop Category 0) and all safety outputs reset to low [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].
  - Recovery mode disables limits for joint position, safety planes and tool orientation; moving the robot in Recovery must be done with caution because those protections are inactive [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
  - Safety plane accuracy and performance characteristics apply (accuracy: 40 mm, PLd, Category 3) — take these limits into account in the risk assessment [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

- Operational notes:
  - Safety planes should be configured as part of the Software Safety Configuration and protected by password control per the integrator’s risk assessment [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
  - Remember the end effector is not monitored by the UR safety system (functioning of the end effector/connection cable is not protected) — include the end effector in your risk assessment and safeguarding decisions [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Use safety planes to bound the workspace and restrict the tool and elbow. Configure up to eight safety planes and set their modes (Normal, Reduced, or Normal & Reduced) to enforce position limits. Tool/Elbow restrictions can be tied to these planes. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable Elbow Restriction to prevent the elbow from passing through defined planes (UR5e elbow restriction radius is 0.13 m). This helps ensure the elbow cannot enter restricted areas. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Use Tool Flange Restriction to keep the tool flange from crossing a safety plane; you can remove the restriction if needed for large tools. This helps keep the end effector within the safe area while enabling tool offsets. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Create and assign a plane feature, then apply it to Safety Planes. This establishes the boundary for both the tool and elbow and supports popup warnings if the boundary is exceeded. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- For specific directional limits, configure Tool Direction and Tool Position restrictions (define the center feature, cone angle, and tool TCP/positions) to constrain where the tool can point and move relative to the planned boundary. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Refer to risk assessment guidance to identify applicable hazards and ensure appropriate safeguards (including safety configuration settings) are in place before operation. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reasons:
- The robot is in Reduced mode or Recovery mode, causing speed reductions or stops to meet safety limits. In Normal mode, safety limits apply; Reduced mode uses stricter limits, and Recovery mode locks movement to bring the arm back within limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- A safety limit or safety plane/limit was triggered or configured to slow/stop motion (e.g., Stopping Time Limit, Stopping Distance Limit, Safety Planes, or Tool/Joints limits). The safety system responds by stopping or slowing to stay within configured limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

What to check and do:
- Verify the active safety mode (Normal vs Reduced) and whether Recovery mode is active, then move within the appropriate limits to exit those modes. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- In PolyScope, check Safety Configuration (Safety -> Software Safety Configuration) and confirm the Safety Checksum matches the expected configuration; ensure no unintended changes or an active Reduced configuration via plane or input. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Review any safety inputs or I/O that could trigger Reduced mode (e.g., Safety input pins or 3PE device) and ensure they are in the expected state. If using a Reduced configuration, either revert to Normal or ensure the risk assessment allows the reduced limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf], [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Use safety planes to create boundary limits for both the elbow and tool. You can define up to eight safety planes and configure them with Restrict Elbow and Tool Flange options. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable Elbow Restriction to prevent the elbow from passing through any defined planes; enable Tool Flange Restriction to keep the tool flange from crossing a safety plane. The tool’s unrestricted area is inside the plane, and can be adjusted with plane features. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- When adding a plane, define the plane feature (to set up the safety plane) and use the copy feature as needed; consider Normal, Reduced, or Normal & Reduced modes to enforce the boundary as the safety state changes. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reasons your UR5e is moving slowly or stopping after you start it, even with risk assessment done:

- The safety configuration is in Reduced mode. Reduced mode can be active if a trigger plane or a safety input switches the system to reduced safety limits, causing slower speeds and decelerations. Check the Safety Parameters and whether Normal or Reduced mode is active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- The safety system is in Recovery mode due to a safety limit violation. In Recovery mode, the robot moves with restricted limits and cannot run programs. Verify which safety limits are active and whether Recovery is engaged. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- A safety limit (e.g., Stop or Speed Limit) or a safety function is constraining motion. The Safety System can reduce speed or stop to keep within configured limits (normal vs reduced, stopping time/distance, tool/elbow limits). Confirm current limits in the Safety Configuration. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- The Safety Checksum or safety password/settings were not applied or unlocked correctly. If safety settings aren’t unlocked/applied, the system may behave as if safety constraints are still in place. Check the Safety Checksum and whether Safety settings are unlocked in PolyScope. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- External safety I/O (Safety I/O, 3PE, Emergency Stop, etc.) configured to limit motion or put the robot into a safeguarded state. Review Safety I/O setup and any connected devices. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

If you want, tell me which mode indicator or safety message you’re seeing in PolyScope, and I can point to the exact setting to check. References: Safety Configuration and Software Safety Configuration sections. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I lock the X axis from rotating on the arm when in freedrive mode?

- In the Freedrive panel, select the desired movement type or use the list of axes to customize movement: choose Translation to allow translation only (no rotation), or toggle the specific axis locks to prevent rotation about X. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]  
(Also see Freedrive use from the Move tab for on-screen Freedrive controls and warnings.) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part02.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Define safety planes and tool TCPs, then enable elbow and/or tool flange restrictions in the Safety settings.

- Create and name the required Features (point or plane) in Installation before unlocking Safety. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]  
- Add Safety Planes (Installation → Safety → Planes), copy a Feature into each plane, and enable the plane and its mode (Normal, Reduced, Trigger Reduced). You can enable "Restrict Elbow" to prevent the elbow joint (modeled as a sphere) from crossing the plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]  
  - Elbow sphere radii: UR5e = 0.13 m (used by the elbow restriction). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Define Tool Position(s) (Installation → Safety → Tool Position): set the TCP position and Radius (0–300 mm). Safety planes operate on the tool sphere you define—the plane prevents any point on that sphere from passing the plane. Ensure a Tool Position is added so planes trigger correctly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes/warnings:
- Safety planes only limit the defined Tool spheres and the elbow, not the entire robot arm; other parts may not be constrained by these planes. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]  
- Create features before unlocking the Safety tab because unlocking powers off the robot and prevents creating new features. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Safety planes limit robot position for the tool/end effector or for both tool/end effector and elbow, but there are several risks you must consider:

- Incorrect or unauthorized configuration can leave hazards unaddressed — always set password protection and configure per the application risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Safety planes have limited accuracy (40 mm) and the robot’s expected stopping travel is taken into account; a limit violation or safety-system fault will trigger a Stop Category 0. Design limits and spacing accordingly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Stopping Time/Distance behavior: the safety system may dynamically reduce speed so the robot can stop within configured stopping time/distance — still include this residual motion in your risk assessment and when defining safety planes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Safety planes may not eliminate other hazards (pinch points, sharp edges, items flying from the end effector); these must be considered in the application risk assessment and may require additional safeguarding. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the limitations of using safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Safety planes only limit the defined Tool spheres and the elbow (they do not limit or guarantee protection for other parts of the robot arm). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- You can define up to eight safety planes; each plane must be based on a previously defined feature (plane/point), and safety-plane configuration requires creating features first because unlocking the Safety tab powers off the robot and prevents moving it. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Safety planes can be configured to restrict tool flange and/or elbow, but:
  - Elbow restriction uses a spherical exclusion with a robot-specific radius (UR5e elbow radius = 0.13 m). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
  - If the tool flange restriction is removed (e.g., for large tool offsets), the tool flange can cross the plane while the attached tool may still be constrained. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Safety planes have limited accuracy and behavior characteristics you must consider:
  - The safety planes’ specified accuracy/performance is 40 mm. [010__L1__10._02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
  - Safety limits (including planes) take expected stopping distance into account; trigger planes include a 20 mm hysteresis band to avoid nuisance stops. [010__L1__10._02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
  - Tool Position must be correctly configured (TCP and tool radius) for a safety plane to trigger correctly. [010__L1__10._04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Deletion and modification notes:
  - Deleting a plane has no undo; if you copy a feature into a plane and later modify the feature, the plane can become out-of-sync and must be re-synced or recreated. [010__L1__10._04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Safety planes restrict only the defined Tool (and optionally the Elbow) spheres, not the overall robot arm; other parts of the arm can still enter the restricted area unless separately prevented [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

- A safety plane does not by itself guarantee that sharp edges, other arm segments, or attached tools cannot expose persons to hazards—incorrect or incomplete configuration can leave residual risks; using incorrect safety parameters can result in hazards that are not reasonably eliminated [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

- Practical risks/behaviour to account for when configuring planes:
  - Safety plane limits take expected stopping distance into account, but plane accuracy/limits have finite tolerances (safety planes listed with 40 mm accuracy) and the system may initiate Stop Category 0 on violations or faults [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].
  - Trigger Reduced Mode: there is a 20 mm zone around a trigger plane where both Normal and Reduced limits are allowed (to avoid nuisance stops) — transitions can take up to 500 ms when using an input to switch reduced/normal, so limits may not be instant [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

  - Elbow restriction uses a ball of defined radius (UR5e 0.13 m); incorrect elbow/tool selections can leave elbow or other links able to pass through planes [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

- Always perform an application risk assessment (ISO 12100 / ISO 10218-2, ISO/TS 15066 guidance) and set/configure safety planes and other safety parameters according to that assessment; unauthorized changes must be prevented by password protection [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the safety system is restricting motion — e.g. the robot is in Reduced or Recovery mode, or stopping-time/distance limits are forcing lower speeds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

Supporting checks you should make:
- Recovery mode at startup: if an active safety limit is violated when powering on, the robot starts in Recovery mode (programs cannot run and motion is limited) — check and move the arm back within limits using Freedrive or the Move tab. Recovery limits are joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Reduced mode or trigger planes: the robot may be using Reduced safety limits because the TCP is beyond a Trigger Reduced plane or a safety input is active; Reduced mode reduces allowed speeds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Stopping time/distance and other safety limits: tight Stopping Time or Stopping Distance settings dynamically reduce max speed so the robot can stop within those limits. Verify those settings in Safety Configuration. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Safety inputs / Safeguard stops: check that no safety input (Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop, Three-Position Enabling Device, etc.) is active or miswired — these can cause Stop Category 0/1/2 and change behavior. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

If after these checks you cannot find the cause, inspect the Safety Checksum and applied Safety Configuration in PolyScope and confirm no unintended safety settings are active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: The robot arm running slowly when started could be due to many potential things.
The speed settings could be turned down.
The environment temperature could be too low or high. Temperatures outside of 0-50C can reduce the speed. 
The robot could be in reduced mode, which can occur when the arm reaches outside it's specified reduced mode safety planes.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the safety system is restricting motion — e.g. the robot is in Reduced or Recovery mode, or stopping-time/distance limits are forcing lower speeds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

Supporting checks you should make:
- Recovery mode at startup: if an active safety limit is violated when powering on, the robot starts in Recovery mode (programs cannot run and motion is limited) — check and move the arm back within limits using Freedrive or the Move tab. Recovery limits are joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Reduced mode or trigger planes: the robot may be using Reduced safety limits because the TCP is beyond a Trigger Reduced plane or a safety input is active; Reduced mode reduces allowed speeds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Stopping time/distance and other safety limits: tight Stopping Time or Stopping Distance settings dynamically reduce max speed so the robot can stop within those limits. Verify those settings in Safety Configuration. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Safety inputs / Safeguard stops: check that no safety input (Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop, Three-Position Enabling Device, etc.) is active or miswired — these can cause Stop Category 0/1/2 and change behavior. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

If after these checks you cannot find the cause, inspect the Safety Checksum and applied Safety Configuration in PolyScope and confirm no unintended safety settings are active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: - Likely cause: the safety system is enforcing its safety limits (Normal or Reduced) or entering Recovery after a limit violation, which can slow or stop motion even if nothing is nearby.

- Key points:
  - The safety functions include Stopping Time Limit and Stopping Distance Limit that dynamically slow the robot so it can stop within the defined limits. If a limit is reached, the robot may stop or slow down as designed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]
  - You can have Normal and Reduced safety parameter configurations. The robot can switch to Reduced mode based on a plane trigger or safety input, with a transition delay (up to 500 ms) when using inputs. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]
  - If a safety limit is exceeded or a fault is detected, the system issues a Stop Category 0 (Recovery may be required to reset). Recovery mode allows manual movement back within limits but disables certain limits temporarily. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp101-107.pdf]
  - Ensure you verify the current safety configuration (Normal vs Reduced) and any active safety inputs or planes that could trigger Reduced mode or recovery. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]

- If you need, I can help you check which safety limits or inputs are active in PolyScope to determine which mechanism is causing the slow-down or stop. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf] [008__L1__8._Installation__pp61-70.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Use Safety Planes to define boundary planes that limit tool and elbow movement. - Enable Elbow Restriction so the elbow cannot pass through any defined safety planes; the elbow clearance radius varies by robot size (e.g., UR5e is 0.13 m). - For precise area control around the end effector, configure Tool Position (TCP) boundaries and use a plane feature to offset the boundary; the tool’s position and radius determine when Reduced mode is triggered by a safety plane. Ensure your feature-based plane and tool position are synced and that the safety configuration includes Normal/Reduced modes as needed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Safety planes restrict the robot workspace by limiting the tool and elbow movement; they do not replace the overall robot limit (they act in Normal/Reduced modes as configured) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf].
- They can be set as Disabled, Normal, Reduced, or Normal & Reduced, and a Trigger Reduced mode can switch the system to Reduced when the tool/elbow crosses the plane [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf].
- Important caveats:
  - Defining safety planes only limits the defined Tool spheres and elbow; other parts of the arm may still reach non-restricted areas [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp121-132.pdf].
  - A tool/tcp must be defined and linked to a feature before configuring planes, and planes may be offset or copied from features; incorrect setup can lead to unintended movements if the limits are not aligned with the actual tool and workpiece [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp121-132.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reasons your UR5e moves slowly or stops on start, even after a risk assessment:
- Safety mode is Reduced or Recovery. In Reduced mode, safety limits are stricter; in Recovery mode, limits are disabled for movement back into safe bounds. Check which safety mode is active and switch back to Normal if appropriate. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Safety limits (Speed, Stopping Time/Distance, Momentum, etc.) may be set conservatively. If Stopping Time Limit or Stopping Distance Limit are active, the robot will slow or stop to ensure it can stop within those limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- The safety configuration or password-protected settings may have changed or not been applied. Verify the Safety Configuration and that changes were Apply’d and Restarted, and confirm the Safety Checksum matches the expected configuration. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- The robot could be in a Reduced configuration triggered by a safety input or by a safety plane, which can cause it to decelerate even if no risk assessment issues are present. Check if a triggerReduced plane or safety input is causing the transition. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__01__10.2._Safety-related_Functions__pp99-106.pdf]

What to check and how to fix:
- Verify current Safety Mode (Normal vs Reduced vs Recovery) in Software Safety Configuration and Safe Home/I/O settings. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Check stopping and speed limits in Safety Configuration; ensure Normal mode limits align with your risk assessment. If needed, adjust within risk-approved values and Apply/Restart. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Confirm Safety Checksum reflects your current configuration. If changes were made, Apply and Restart and verify the Checksum shows as expected. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- If using safety I/O, ensure no safety input (e.g., a Reduced or recovery trigger) is active inadvertently via Safety I/O configuration. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

Note: The end effector is not covered by UR safety system, so ensure all external hazards and device interactions are included in risk assessment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__01__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: I dropped some liquid on my robot arm. Will that break it or cause a safety issue?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer:
Possibly — it depends on where the liquid reached and whether the environment exceeded the equipment IP ratings. The robot arm is rated IP54, but the Control Box is IP44; the Control Box must not come into contact with liquids. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:

- A wet Control Box can cause fatal injury — keep the Control Box and cables away from liquids. If the Control Box has been exposed to liquid, do not operate it. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- If you suspect liquid reached electrical parts, power the robot down and disconnect mains (press power off on the Teach Pendant, unplug the mains cable, allow 30 seconds for stored energy to discharge) before further inspection or service. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

QUESTION: I dropped some liquid on my robot arm. Will that break it or cause a safety issue?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possibly — it depends on amount/location of liquid and whether the robot exceeds its IP rating. The robot arm is rated IP54, so small splashes may be tolerated, but the Control Box is only IP44 and must not get wet. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Recommended immediate actions:
- Power down and isolate mains (press Teach Pendant power button, unplug mains) and allow ~30 seconds for stored energy to discharge before touching or servicing. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Do not operate the robot if any part (especially the Control Box or cables) is wet; keep the Control Box and cables away from liquids to avoid fatal electrical hazard. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Visually inspect for contamination or damage; if liquid entered connectors or the Control Box, do not power up and contact service (the sources advise placing equipment in environments suited to their IP ratings). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

If you need specific remediation steps after a spill (drying, inspection, service), the provided sources do not give further detail.

QUESTION: What should I do to avoid a pinching hazard?
STUDENT ANSWER: Remove or relocate obstacles, reposition the robot, or use safety planes and joint limits to prevent the robot entering the pinching hazard areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- CAUTION: placing the robot in certain areas can create pinching hazards that can lead to injury—address them during the application risk assessment and safety configuration. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: The robot is likely obeying a configured safety limit (e.g., Speed/Stopping limits, Reduced mode) or has entered Recovery or a safety stop; these modes will slow or stop motion even if no obstacle is near. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Possible causes (check these): 
- Safety limits (Tool Speed, Elbow Speed, Stopping Time/Distance) are set so the controller reduces maximum speed to guarantee it can stop within the configured stopping time/distance. Lower stopping time/distance settings reduce allowable speed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- The robot is in Reduced mode (trigger plane or safety input active), which uses more restrictive speed/momentum limits. The controller transitions to/from Reduced mode and adapts limits within up to 500 ms. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Recovery mode is active because a safety limit was violated (including on power-up); Recovery applies fixed, limited joint/speed/force values and disables some position/orientation limits, allowing only restricted motion until you move back within limits or clear the fault. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- A Safeguard Stop, Emergency Stop, or other safety input/output state is active, which will pause or stop programs (Stop Category 1/2/0 depending on trigger). Verify safety inputs/outputs and that no safety I/O is asserting a stop. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- A change in I/O during program execution will stop the program (I/O Tab updates at 10 Hz and program pauses if I/O is changed). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part02.pdf]

What to check next:
- Inspect Safety Configuration (Normal/Reduced limits, Stopping Time/Distance, Tool/Elbow speed) and the Safety Checksum in PolyScope. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Verify no safety inputs are asserted (Emergency Stop, Safeguard Reset, Reduced input, 3PE, etc.), and check safety I/O wiring. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]  
- Check if the controller started in Recovery mode (indicated by restricted movement limits) and move the arm back within limits or clear the condition per the manual. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

If you cannot find the cause from the above, say so and provide any observed indicators (Safety Checksum, which safety mode is shown, any safety outputs active) so I can point to the exact setting to inspect.

- After a spill, treat it as a safety and electrical risk and avoid moving or powering the system until it has been inspected and cleared by a qualified person. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

  - Use Tool Position and Copy TCP to accurately define the tool’s boundary within the plane, ensuring the safety system triggers when the TCP approaches the plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Note: Defining safety planes only limits the defined tool spheres and elbow, not the robot’s overall arm limit; ensure planes are configured with the appropriate mode and that the elbow/tool flange restrictions are active for your boundary. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: To keep the elbow and tool inside a defined boundary, use safety planes and tool/elbow restrictions:

- Define safety planes: you can create up to eight planes to restrict the tool and elbow. Enable Elbow Restriction to prevent the elbow from crossing the planes, and enable Tool Flange Restriction to keep the tool from crossing a plane. Planes are configured under Safety > Planes, and you copy a feature into the plane configuration before enabling restrictions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Use the Elbow and Tool Flange restrictions: enabling Elbow Restriction stops the elbow from passing through any defined planes; Tool Flange Restriction prevents the tool flange (and attached tool) from crossing a safety plane. The tool flange may be left unrestricted if you need more clearance for large tools. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Configure the plane features carefully: add a plane feature, offset as needed, and apply displacement so the plane bounds the desired area. You can adjust which parts trigger the plane (Elbow, Tool Flange) per your application. If you delete or modify features, ensure the Safety plane configuration remains in sync. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Optional: use Tool Position limits to define tool spheres and their relation to the safety planes; ensure a Tool Position is set so the safety planes trigger correctly as the TCP approaches them. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes:
- Safety planes provide position-based boundary limits but do not override the overall robot arm limits. Planes constrain the tool/elbow within defined regions, in conjunction with the elbow and tool flange restrictions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Pinch hazards in the workspace can occur if the robot moves into areas defined by safety planes. Use safety planes and joint limits to eliminate or reduce these hazards.
- Two identified pinch-hazard zones: (1) a left radial-motion area when the wrist 1 joint is at least 750 mm from the base, and (2) a right tangential area within 200 mm of the base.
- A risk assessment should be performed before operation to determine appropriate safeguarding and settings. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: - It’s likely that the safety system is in Normal, Reduced, or Recovery mode, and in Reduced or Recovery mode the robot slows or restricts motion. Check which safety mode is active.

- If Reduced mode is active, the system uses reduced safety limits (including lower speeds) and may switch automatically when a trigger plane or a safety input moves the configuration to Reduced. This can cause slower motion or stopping as you start moving. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- If Recovery mode is active, the robot enforces a fixed, non-customizable set of safety limits and may restrict movement while you’re returning back inside the limits. The recovery state is entered after a safety limit is violated or at startup if limits are already violated. Move back within the limits carefully (manual/Freedrive allowed as specified). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- How to confirm and adjust:
  - In PolyScope, check Safety Configuration -> Safety Modes to see whether Normal, Reduced, or Recovery is active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
  - Verify the Safety Checksum to ensure the safety configuration you expect is applied. After changes, apply/restart and visually inspect safety configuration as described. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
  - Check for any Trigger Reduced plane or safety inputs that might switch you to Reduced mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- If needed, review I/O configurations and any external inputs that could trigger Reduced or Recovery modes via Safety I/O. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Safety planes are used to prevent the robot from entering hazardous workspace areas, primarily to avoid pinching hazards. You must be aware that:

- Pinching hazards: the robot can pinch body parts in certain radial and near-base tangential areas; safety planes (and joint limits) are used to prevent the robot moving into those areas.  
- Other related risks that safety planes help mitigate include contact injuries (bruising, sprain or fracture) and exposure to sharp edges or points on the tool/end effector or nearby obstacles.  
- Safety planes are only one part of the application risk assessment — also consider loose bolts, items falling or being ejected, mistaken understanding of emergency stops, and incorrect or unauthorized changes to safety configuration parameters.

Always remove obstacles or reposition the robot where possible, and set appropriate safety planes and joint limits as part of the application risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Safety planes are used to prevent the robot from entering hazardous areas (for example to avoid pinching zones) but you must account for the risks the safety planes are intended to mitigate and risks introduced by incorrect configuration:

- Safety planes should be used together with joint limits to eliminate pinch hazards (areas described for radial motion when wrist 1 ≥ 750 mm from base, and within 200 mm of the base when moving tangentially). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Consider potential harms the safety planes must address: penetration by sharp edges/points, bruising from contact, sprain or bone fracture from impact, and items falling or flying from the end effector. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Manage hazards related to safety-plane configuration: incorrect safety-configuration parameters, and unauthorized changes (so always enable password protection and manage access). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Also consider human factors and system-level issues such as mistaken understanding of what is controlled by multiple emergency stops. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Always perform an application risk assessment (integrator’s responsibility) using ISO 12100/ISO 10218-2 (and ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative cases) before first power-on. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.

- Position/orientation limits (joint, elbow, tool) can also prevent or slow movements toward configured forbidden areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes plus elbow and tool flange restrictions in the Safety configuration.

Key points
- Define a feature (point or plane) in Installation > Features before editing Safety; once Safety is unlocked the robot powers off and you cannot create new features [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Create up to eight safety planes (Installation > Safety > Planes), copy the relevant feature into the plane and set the plane Mode (Disabled / Normal / Reduced / Normal & Reduced / Trigger Reduced) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Enable “Restrict Elbow” on a plane to prevent the elbow joint from passing through that plane (UR5e elbow restriction ball radius = 0.13 m) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Enable “Restrict Tool Flange” (and define a Tool Position/TCP and radius) to prevent the tool flange or the defined tool sphere from crossing the plane; set the tool radius and position so the sphere correctly represents the dangerous part of the tool [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Note: safety planes only limit the defined tool spheres and elbow, not the entire robot arm; other parts of the arm may not obey the plane unless additional measures are used [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  

Recommended short procedure
1. Create/name the plane feature in Installation > Features.  
2. Installation > Safety > Planes: Add plane, Copy Feature = your feature, set Mode and side allowed.  
3. Check “Restrict Elbow” (UR5e radius 0.13 m) if you must block elbow crossing.  
4. Under Tool Position add or edit the tool TCP and set an appropriate radius and offset so the tool sphere matches the hazardous part. Apply changes.  
5. Verify in the graphics pane and test in Normal/Reduced modes.  

Also perform an application risk assessment and set password protection for safety configuration changes as part of the integration responsibility [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Direct answer
- Safety planes can limit robot position but if configured incorrectly or violated they can create hazards (e.g., unexpected motion or failure to stop) or nuisance stops; a limit violation triggers a Stop Category 0. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting points
- Incorrect setting or unauthorized changes to safety planes can leave risks uneliminated or insufficiently reduced — always include safety-planes in the application risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- The safety plane function has a documented accuracy (40 mm) and the robot’s stopping distance/time must be taken into account when defining planes; the system dynamically reduces speed so limits aren’t exceeded. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Workspace pinching hazards remain relevant near the base and at certain radial positions; use planes and joint limits to prevent the robot entering pinching areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the limitations of using safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Direct answer:
- Safety planes only limit the defined Tool spheres and the elbow, not the overall robot arm; other parts of the arm may not obey the plane [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Safety planes have a positional accuracy/limit of 40 mm (safety function accuracy) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

Supporting points:
- You can define up to eight safety planes; each can restrict tool and/or elbow and can be enabled/disabled or set to trigger Reduced mode. Deleting a plane has no undo (must be remade) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Tool flange versus tool-sphere behavior: restricting the tool flange prevents the flange and attached tool from crossing a plane; removing flange restriction lets the flange cross while the defined tool sphere remains constrained — you must set a Tool Position for planes to trigger correctly [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Elbow restriction uses a spherical exclusion (UR5e radius = 0.13 m) and can be disabled if elbow passage is required [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Trigger planes can switch the safety system to Reduced mode; there is a 20 mm band around a trigger plane where both Normal and Reduced limits are allowed to avoid nuisance stops [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].
- Safety planes are feature-based: you must create and name features before unlocking the Safety Tab because the robot powers off when the Safety Tab is unlocked and the arm cannot be moved [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the robot’s safety configuration is limiting its motion—built-in functions can automatically reduce speed or stop the robot to ensure configured limits are not exceeded. For example, Force and power limiting, Momentum limiting and Speed limitation reduce motion in case of collisions or high energy; Stopping Time Limit and Stopping Distance Limit automatically affect the robot speed and stopping to ensure the limits are respected (the safety control does continuous monitoring). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Also check for incorrect or unauthorized changes to safety parameters (unauthorized access can change settings); always enable password protection for safety configuration. If the settings look correct but the behavior continues, verify the safety configuration and stopping-category behavior described in the manual. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

If you cannot find a relevant safety parameter in the configuration, say so and I can guide which settings to inspect next.

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Set up Safety Planes and Tool Position/Tool Direction limits in the Safety configuration so the elbow and tool are restricted to the required area.

Supporting points:
- Create a plane feature in Installation > Features, then add Safety Planes (Installation > Safety > Planes). Configure the plane’s mode and enable "Restrict Elbow" to prevent the elbow joint from passing through the plane (UR5e elbow ball radius = 0.13 m) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Restrict the Tool Flange (Tool Position / add a Tool and set Radius/Position) to prevent the tool flange or defined tool sphere from crossing a safety plane; ensure you define the Tool Position so safety planes trigger correctly [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Use Tool Direction limits (cone center and cone angle) to constrain the angle the tool may point, if needed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  

Note: Safety planes only limit defined Tool spheres and elbow, not all other robot parts—verify your risk assessment and configuration cover all hazards [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Direct answer:
Safety planes can restrict the tool and/or elbow but do not guarantee other parts of the robot arm are prevented from entering the restricted area; you must account for remaining hazards like pinching, elbow/tool geometry, and stopping distance when using safety planes [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

Supporting points:

- Trigger planes switch between Normal and Reduced safety parameter sets (with a 20 mm overlap area to avoid nuisance stops), and switching via inputs can take up to 500 ms to take effect—account for this in the risk assessment and stopping performance calculations [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the robot is operating under configured safety limits or has entered a safety/Recovery state that reduces or stops motion. Check these items in your safety configuration and status: [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Safety functions such as force & power limiting, momentum limiting and speed limitation will reduce speed or clamp motion to limit energy transfer per the application risk assessment [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Stopping Time Limit or Stopping Distance Limit settings automatically reduce the robot speed to ensure the configured stop limits are not exceeded [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- If a safety limit has been exceeded, the system can automatically enter Recovery Mode (a Manual Mode) where joint speed is limited to 30°/s, tool speed to 250 mm/s, force to 100 N, momentum to 10 kg·m/s and power to 80 W; the robot may also issue a Stop Category 0 if violations occur [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].  
- Verify which safety inputs/outputs are active and whether an emergency stop, Three-Position Enabling Device, or other external safety device is engaged or latched (E-stop must be manually reset) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf; 003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].

If these checks do not explain the behavior, the safety configuration parameters may need review or an additional safety input is being triggered; the integrator/user is responsible for verifying the safety settings per the application risk assessment [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: I dropped some liquid on my robot arm. Will that break it or cause a safety issue?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: Possibly — it depends where and how much liquid. The robot arm is rated IP54 (protection against splashing), but the Control Box is only IP44 and “a wet Control Box can cause fatal injury.” [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Small splashes onto the robot arm are within the IP54 rating (splash protection); immersion or large amounts of liquid can exceed the rating and may damage components or create safety hazards. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Never let liquids contact the Control Box; if the Control Box gets wet, power down and isolate immediately because a wet Control Box can cause fatal injury. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- If liquid was spilled: power down the robot using the prescribed procedure (power off on Teach Pendant, unplug mains, wait ~30 seconds to discharge), then allow equipment to dry and have a qualified person inspect before re-powering. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use Safety Planes with Elbow and Tool/Tool‑flange restrictions, and define the tool position/sphere so the safety system enforces the boundary.

How to (high level)
- Define a plane feature in Installation > General (feature must exist before editing Safety). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- In Installation > Safety > Planes, Add plane and Copy Feature, then enable:
  - Restrict Elbow to prevent the elbow joint from passing through the plane. (Elbow ball radius for UR5e = 0.13 m.) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
  - Restrict Tool Flange (or configure an unrestricted flange with a defined tool) so the tool flange / tool sphere cannot cross the plane. [010__L1__10._10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Define the tool in Installation > Safety > Tool Position, set the TCP position and Radius (sphere). Safety planes use that sphere when detecting and preventing crossings. Ensure a Tool Position is set so planes trigger correctly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Choose plane Modes (Normal, Reduced, Trigger Reduced, etc.) to control when the plane is active and whether it only triggers Reduced mode or enforces a strict limit. [010__L1__10._10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes and warnings
- Safety planes limit the defined Tool spheres and elbow, not every other part of the arm — defining a plane does not guarantee other parts of the arm obey it. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Configure and apply safety settings only after an application risk assessment and with Safety password protection enabled. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: Safety planes only restrict the defined Tool spheres and the elbow — they do not guarantee other parts of the robot arm will obey the plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Safety planes act on defined tool TCP spheres and (optionally) the elbow; other robot parts are not constrained by the plane (so a plane does not guarantee all parts stay out of the restricted area). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- You must define features and tool positions/TCPs before configuring planes (and add a tool under Tool Flange) for planes and trigger behavior to work correctly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Practical limits: up to eight safety planes; elbow restriction uses a spherical exclusion whose radius is robot-specific (UR5e elbow radius = 0.13 m); safety plane positional accuracy is specified as 40 mm in the safety function table. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Behavior near trigger planes: Trigger Reduced planes have a 20 mm transition band where both normal and reduced limits are allowed, and switching to Reduced via an input can take up to 500 ms to become active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely the safety system is limiting motion (speed reduction or stop) because a safety limit, safety configuration, or initialization check is triggered.

Possible causes to check:
- The robot is in Recovery or Reduced mode due to a safety limit or configuration (Recovery enforces strict limits: 30°/s joint speed, 250 mm/s tool speed, etc.) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- A safety parameter (Stopping Time/Stopping Distance, Speed Limit, Joint Speed Limit, Force/Momentum/Power limits) is configured to values that dynamically reduce speed to ensure the robot can stop within the limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- Initialization detected a mounting/installation mismatch (if the mounting verification fails, the Start button is disabled) [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- A safety input/output (Emergency Stop, Safeguard, Reduced Mode input, Three‑Position Enabling Device, etc.) is active or stuck, or an external safety signal is causing Reduced limits or a stop [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf].

What to do next (short checklist):
- Check PolyScope for Recovery/Reduced mode status and any safety limit violation messages [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- Verify safety inputs/outputs and emergency stops are not active and test them per commissioning steps [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf].  
- Confirm mounting verification passed during startup (no Start-button disable due to a >30° mismatch) [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Review your configured safety limits (speed, stopping time/distance, joint limits, force/momentum/power) to ensure they match the application risk assessment and intended normal mode [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

If none of the above is evident, the sources do not provide further troubleshooting steps.

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes and related restrictions to keep the elbow and tool inside defined boundaries.

- Create up to eight safety planes in Safety > Planes and configure each with Normal/Reduced modes as needed. Use Copy Feature to base planes on a defined feature. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Enable Elbow Restriction and Tool Flange Restriction to prevent the elbow or tool from crossing a safety plane. The UR5e elbow-restriction radius is 0.13 m (UR5e; see robot-specific setting in urcontrol.conf). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Use Tool Position and Tool Direction limits to constrain the tool’s location and orientation relative to the defined planes. Define a TCP/tool position within the safety settings and set a Tool Direction limit (cone) if needed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes:
- Defining safety planes limits the movement within those planes but does not guarantee the entire robot arm stays within the boundary; other parts may still move outside the plane. Planes act as restrictive limits on the tool/elbow relative to the defined features. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes and tool/elbow restrictions to keep the elbow and tool within a defined area.

- Configure safety planes to limit the workspace for the tool and elbow. You can add up to eight planes and set their mode (Normal, Reduced, etc.) to constrain movement. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable elbow and tool flange restrictions so the tool flange and attached tool cannot cross a safety plane. You can remove or apply restrictions as needed for large tools. The elbow restriction radius for UR5e is 0.13 m. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Use Tool Position restrictions to define up to two Tool Center Points (TCPs) and associated radii. The safety system uses these TCP positions and radii to enforce stopping distances and tool/plane interactions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- If needed, adjust Safety Planes and Tool/Elbow limits in the Safety configuration to ensure the applied limits (speed, momentum, stopping distance/time, etc.) prevent the tool or elbow from entering restricted zones. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- For risk guidance and to prevent hazards, include these boundary considerations in your risk assessment (pinching hazards near the elbow/workpiece). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the limitations of using safety planes?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Safety planes can only limit the tool and the elbow from going beyond the plane. Other parts of the arm cannot be configured to respect safety planes.
STUDENT ANSWER: - Safety planes only limit the defined Tool spheres and elbow; they do not enforce an overall limit on the entire robot arm. In other words, specifying a plane does not guarantee the rest of the arm will stay within that boundary. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Supporting points:
- A plane can be configured with Normal, Reduced, or Normal & Reduced modes, but these restrictions apply only to the tool/elbow within the plane, not to the entire arm. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Tool flange and elbow restrictions are set per plane and can be enabled/disabled as needed. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]
- Removing a tool/flange restriction or adjusting planes requires additional configuration and does not retroactively enforce global arm limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: - Likely cause: safety configuration limits are restricting motion. The safety functions (Speed Limit, Stopping Time Limit, Stopping Distance Limit, Force/Momentum, safety planes) are designed to reduce risk and can slow or stop motion if limits are reached or configured for reduced safety. Check the Safety Function Set and Safety Parameter Set (Normal vs Reduced) in Safety-related Functions and Interfaces. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]

- If a safety limit was exceeded, Recovery Mode may be active, which stops program execution until the issue is resolved. In Recovery Mode, you cannot run programs and must move the arm back within limits (Freedrive/Move tab) before resuming. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

- What to verify next:
  - Ensure you are operating under Normal safety parameters (not Reduced) and that Safety Planes, Joint/Tool speed limits, and other limits are appropriate for your task. If a Reduced configuration is active, switch to Normal as per the safety parameter set. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]
  - Check whether Recovery Mode is active and, if so, move back within limits using Freedrive or the Move tab, then restart the program. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

If these checks don’t resolve the issue, there may be a fault or misconfiguration triggering a safety stop; consult the commissioning/tests guidance to verify safety inputs/outputs and mode transitions. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely because either the joint brakes are being released during start-up or the robot/stand is resonating; both can cause the robot to vibrate. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf] [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Slight vibrations are normal when joint brakes are released during robot start-up/initialization. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- If the stand lacks sufficient dynamic stiffness or its eigenfrequency matches the robot motion frequency, the system can resonate and appear to vibrate; the stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Vibrations can also occur in situations such as being close to collision or when using Freedrive/Backdrive; these may be undesirable and are described in the Freedrive/Backdrive sections. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

QUESTION: How can I reduce the force applied to the operator in case of a collision?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use the robot’s safety configuration to limit energy transfer (force, power, momentum and speed) and to restrict motions and orientations of the arm and end effector. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Supporting measures:
- Enable Force and power limiting to reduce clamping forces and pressures in collisions. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use Momentum limiting to reduce transient impact energy by lowering robot speed on collisions. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Apply Speed limitation to ensure tool speed stays below configured limits. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use Joint, elbow and tool/end effector position limiting and Tool/end effector orientation limiting to avoid motions or orientations that increase risk (e.g., prevent sharp edges pointing toward the operator). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Employ Power and Force Limiting (PFL) safety functions (inherent design/control) as part of the application so any exceeded parameter causes a robot stop. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Always determine and configure these settings as part of the application risk assessment and validate them for your specific end effector and workpiece. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
