QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
STUDENT ANSWER: Shifting the payload center of gravity (CoG) away from the tool flange reduces the robot’s rated payload capacity and can reduce the robot’s ability to accelerate. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Supporting points:
- The rated payload depends on the CoG offset; larger offsets reduce allowable payload (see payload vs. CoG graph). [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]
- The robot can accommodate long CoG offsets better if the payload is placed below the tool flange, but capacity to accelerate can still be reduced if the CoG exceeds the robot’s reach/payload. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: The offset for the center of gravity can affect the way the arm moves due to what it expects the object's center to be.

Too great of a center of gravity, or too much weight can result in tipping hazards.

- The rated payload depends on the CoG offset; larger offsets reduce allowable payload (see payload vs. CoG graph). [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]
- The robot can accommodate long CoG offsets better if the payload is placed below the tool flange, but capacity to accelerate can still be reduced if the CoG exceeds the robot’s reach/payload. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]
- To avoid stops and ensure optimal motion, configure the controller with the correct payload mass, CoG and inertia (use Set Payload or the Payload Estimation Wizard). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Likely causes
- The robot approached a singularity, which can make the arm “feel heavy” and produce very sudden, fast motions as it moves through the singular pose [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- A safety event (limit violation, emergency/safeguard stop or fault) and subsequent restart/backdrive can produce strong movements or vibrations when the arm is moved or when power is restored (backdrive/full restart can cause vibrations) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

How to prevent it
- Avoid poses and motion sequences that produce singularities; do not program motions that can cause a singularity [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Use and configure the robot’s safety functions (joint position limits, joint speed limit, safety planes, tool orientation, speed/force/momentum/power limits) according to your application risk assessment so the system limits dangerous motion before it occurs [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
  - For hand-guiding/linear manual use, ensure the speed limit for tool/elbow is set to ≤250 mm/s unless risk assessment permits higher [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- If an emergency stop was involved, always visually identify and fix the cause before resetting the E-stop; reset only at the push‑button that latched it [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- Where movement after a stop is undesirable, use Backdrive procedures cautiously (robot feels “heavy” and full restart can cause vibrations); test Backdrive on all joints and follow the prescribed sequences [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

If you cannot determine the root cause from these checks, the sources do not provide further diagnostic steps.

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes include insufficient stand/support stiffness or resonance, brake release/backdrive during start-up or freedrive, and singularity-related behaviour.

Supporting points:
- A stand that is not sufficiently stiff can deflect or resonate (minimum resonance frequency 45 Hz recommended), causing the robot to appear to vibrate; ensure the mounting surface meets torque and weight requirements and is vibration-free [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Minor vibrations can occur when joint brakes are released during initialization or when using Backdrive/Freedrive; this is normal but may be undesirable near collisions (use Backdrive to control specific joints) [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf, 007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Approaching a singularity increases resistance and can cause sudden or fast motions that feel like vibration; avoid programming poses that can cause singularities [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot’s rated payload and dynamic performance depend on the payload center of gravity (CoG) offset. If you offset the CoG:

- The rated payload changes with CoG offset — you must account for the distance from the tool flange when computing allowable payload [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf].  
- The controller will automatically reduce accelerations if the payload CoG (and mass/inertia) are not correctly configured, so capacity to accelerate can be reduced if the CoG exceeds the robot’s reach/payload [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf].  
- Configure the payload mass, CoG and inertia in PolyScope (or use the Payload Estimation Wizard) and use Set Payload nodes in your program to avoid unexpected robot stops and ensure optimal motion [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: Sudden strong movement can be caused by the robot approaching a singularity or by transitions related to safety stops and restarts (e.g., recovery or restart after a stop), both of which can produce heavy, fast, or vibrating joint behaviour. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting points / how to prevent it:
- Singularity: a pose near a singularity "can stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements"; avoid programming motions that approach singularity poses. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Safety-stop / restart behaviour: if a safety limit is violated the controller issues stops and may enter Recovery mode or perform a stop category; restarting or recovering can produce vibrations or heavy joint feel (and sudden motion if limits are not respected). Use Recovery/Freedrive procedures only with caution. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Configure and use safety limits: set appropriate Joint Position Limits, Joint Speed Limit, Safety Planes, Tool Orientation, Speed/Force/Momentum/Power limits, and Stopping Time/Distance to limit possible post-stop motion and reduce energy transferred in collisions. Verify the settings per your risk assessment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Risk assessment and verification: perform the integrator's application risk assessment before first power-up, lock safety configuration with a password, and verify/test safety functions regularly. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Mechanical/installation checks: ensure the robot is mounted on a stiff, stable stand and avoid resonance (minimum stand resonance ~45 Hz) so unexpected dynamics do not amplify motions. Also check for collisions/obstacles that might trigger protective stops. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

If you need, tell me what stop category or message PolyScope showed and whether the arm was near any obstacles or unusual poses when it stopped; I can point to the most likely specific setting to adjust.

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
STUDENT ANSWER: There are three stop categories defined (IEC 60204-1):

- Stop Category 0 — Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 1 — Stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 2 — Stop the robot while maintaining drive power (trajectory may be maintained); drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Typical safety triggers and their stop-category reactions: Emergency Stop → Stop Category 1; Safeguard Stop → Stop Category 2; 3PE Stop → Stop Category 2; Limit violation or safety-system fault → Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reasons your UR5e arm appears to vibrate:

- Normal startup behavior: during boot, when brakes are released, the robot may vibrate and make clicking sounds as brakes release. This is expected as the system transitions to Idle/Ready. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Stand or mounting resonance: if the stand or mounting is not sufficiently stiff, the system can deflect or resonate, causing visible vibration. Ensure the stand is dimensioned for static and dynamic stiffness and that resonance frequency is not met or exceeded. Minimum recommended resonance frequency is 45 Hz. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- High accelerations or improper installation: excessively high accelerations or insecure mounting can amplify vibrations and may trigger safety stops or instability. Verify the robot is securely mounted and consider reducing joint accelerations if needed. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Verification of payload and installation: incorrect payload or mounting can affect motion and cause unexpected motion or vibration. Verify payload and installation settings before operation. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

If the vibration persists beyond initial startup and after confirming secure mounting and correct payload, re-evaluate stand stiffness and potential resonance with the load and operating space. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- An Emergency Stop or Safeguard Stop was triggered (Stop Category 1 or 2). The robot will stop, and depending on the event, may require reset or further action before movement resumes. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- A safety limit violation or fault detected by the safety system can trigger a Stop Category 0 and may result in a sudden movement when the system recovers or is cleared. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]
- Recovery Mode can automatically activate when a safety limit is exceeded, allowing manual movement back within limits but preventing program execution. This can feel like a strong, unexpected movement if the arm moves to rejoin limits. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

How to prevent it (concise guidance):
- Ensure proper operation of safety devices and reset procedures after an E-stop or Safeguard Stop, and verify the reason before resetting. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Configure safety parameters (Normal vs Reduced) and safety limits (Stopping Time, Stopping Distance, Speed/Force limits) according to the risk assessment to ensure the robot can be stopped safely within defined bounds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]
- Perform a thorough risk assessment and use safety planes, Three-Position Enabling Device (if installed), and appropriate safety inputs/outputs to prevent unintended movements. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]

Cited sources:
- Emergency Events and recovery modes: [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Safety functions, parameter sets, and recovery details: [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: - The 3PE buttons have three positions:
  - Position 1 Release: no pressure; robot movement stops in Manual mode, brakes remain released.
  - Position 2 Light-press: presses to a middle point; allows program to play in Manual mode.
  - Position 3 Tight-press: fully pressed; robot movement stops in Manual mode (3PE Stop).

- The functions are active in Manual mode; in Automatic mode 3PE button actions are not used for movement. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: - It can be normal during initial startup: when the Brakes are released, the robot arm may vibrate slightly and make clicking sounds as it starts up. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

- If the vibration continues while running, check the mounting/stand: ensure the stand is sturdy, free of external vibrations, and dimensioned for the loads; a lack of static/dynamic stiffness can cause the arm to vibrate or resonate. The stand should have adequate rigidity and a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- Also verify payload and safety-related factors: incorrect payload/CoG or approaching a singularity can affect motion and feel, so confirm payload settings and avoid singularity poses. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf], [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
STUDENT ANSWER: - An offset center of gravity (CoG) affects the robot’s effective payload and acceleration. The controller automatically adjusts accelerations based on the payload mass, CoG, and inertia, so large CoG offsets can reduce performance or cause stops if not configured correctly. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]
- You can measure and configure CoG using the Payload settings (CX, CY, CZ) and the Payload Estimation Wizard to ensure accurate motion, especially when the payload is extended below the tool flange. The robot can handle a long CoG offset when the payload is placed below the tool flange. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?

QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
STUDENT ANSWER: If you offset the payload center of gravity (CoG), the robot’s rated payload and acceleration capability change — a larger CoG offset reduces the robot’s effective payload and can reduce its capacity to accelerate. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Supporting points:
- The rated payload depends on the CoG offset from the tool flange; the robot can accommodate long offsets better if the payload is placed below the tool flange. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]  
- If the payload CoG exceeds the robot’s reach and payload, the robot’s capacity to accelerate can be reduced. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]  
- Configure payload mass, CoG and inertia correctly (or use the Payload Estimation Wizard) so the controller can automatically adjust accelerations and avoid unexpected robot stops. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely cause: the robot approached a singularity — as the arm nears a singularity it can "stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements" [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

How to prevent it:
- Avoid programming motions that result in poses that can cause a singularity (re‑route paths or change joint configurations) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Use safety limits (joint limits, safety planes) and proper safety configuration determined by an application risk assessment to restrict motion into hazardous poses [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Perform a full application risk assessment and configure/password‑protect safety settings so changes cannot be made inadvertently [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

If this does not match your incident (for example if it followed an emergency stop or power event), inspect emergency/stop history and safety settings as part of troubleshooting [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely causes:

- Resonance of the stand or mounting (insufficient dynamic stiffness): if the stand’s eigenfrequency matches the robot movement frequency the system can resonate, creating the impression the robot arm is vibrating. The stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Normal startup/brake release vibrations: during initialization the robot may vibrate or make slight movements as the joint brakes are released — this is normal when you press Start [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Inadequate/static stiffness or insecure mounting: a stand that is not sufficiently stiff can deflect during motion and cause vibration-like behavior; ensure the robot is secured to a sturdy, vibration-free surface and tightened per mounting instructions (four M8 bolts at 20 Nm) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

If the vibration is unexpected or safety-related, power down and inspect mounting and surroundings before restarting [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

The greater the center of gravity is offset from the origin, the more the capacity of the arm to accelerate can be reduced. 
Too great of a center of gravity, or too much weight can result in tipping hazards.
STUDENT ANSWER: Offsetting the center of gravity changes the robot’s rated payload capability and how the controller handles motion: a larger CoG offset reduces the robot’s capacity to accelerate and may reduce performance or cause robot stops if not configured correctly. Configure the payload mass, Center of Gravity and inertia in PolyScope (or use the Payload Estimation Wizard) so the controller can automatically adjust accelerations; placing the CoG below the tool flange lets the robot accommodate longer offsets more easily. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: Are there risks associated with using 12V vs 24V?
STUDENT ANSWER: Yes. Programmer or wiring errors can cause the voltage to change from 12V to 24V, which can lead to fire damage — verify the use of 12V and proceed with caution. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Tool I/O supply mode must be set in the GUI to 0V, 12V or 24V and the electrical limits (voltage/current) differ for 12V vs 24V operation — configure correctly to avoid damage [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- Digital/analogue I/O and tool outputs have specific voltage/current specifications and some outputs are not current-limited; incorrect wiring or exceeding specs can cause permanent damage or hazards [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- Electrical safety practices (proper grounding, fusing, RCD, and lockout during service) must be followed to reduce electrical/fire risk when using any supply voltage [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely causes are the robot approaching a singularity or a safety limit/stop event (and subsequent Recovery or backdrive behavior) that produced sudden joint motion or high joint torques. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

To prevent recurrence:
- Avoid poses that cause singularities and do not program motions that approach them (singularity can make the arm stop or move suddenly). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Configure appropriate safety limits (tool/elbow speed, joint limits, safety planes, force/momentum/power limits) based on a proper application risk assessment; these limits reduce speed/energy and trigger safe stops before hazardous motion. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Use Stopping Time/Stopping Distance limits (or lower acceleration settings) so the controller limits maximum speed to ensure stopping within configured bounds. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Lock safety settings with a Safety password and follow the integrator’s risk assessment before changing safety parameters. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- If a stop occurred, inspect whether the event was an Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop or a Limit Violation and follow the prescribed reset/recovery procedure; be cautious when moving the arm in Recovery or Backdrive modes (limits such as joint position/orientation may be disabled). [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

If you can provide the exact stop category shown on the Teach Pendant or whether Recovery/Backdrive was used, I can point to the specific reset and configuration steps.

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
STUDENT ANSWER: There are three stop categories (per IEC 60204‑1):

- Stop Category 0: stop by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 1: stop in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 2: stop the robot while drive power is maintained (trajectory may be maintained); Universal Robots’ Category 2 stops are further described as SS1 or SS2 per IEC 61800‑5‑2. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Supporting detail: the safety system will initiate Stop Category 0 for limit violations or safety faults, while an Emergency Stop initiates a Stop Category 1. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons are a three-position enabling device on the Teach Pendant that control robot motion in Manual mode: [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

- Release (no pressure): robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (power retained, brakes released).  
- Light-press (middle position): allows a program to play/run when the robot is in Manual mode.  
- Tight-press (fully pressed): stops robot movement in Manual mode and places the robot in 3PE Stop.  

Additional notes: the 3PE buttons are only active in Manual mode; they are used for Freedrive and Backdrive sequences (specific press/release patterns are required to enter Freedrive/Backdrive). QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: When the 3PE button is not pressed, the robot movement is stopped, power is not removed from the robot arm, and the brakes are release. When there is light pressure the current program can play while the mode is set to manual. When there is tight pressure the robot movement is stopped in manual mode, and the robot is in 3PE stop mode. If you light press it twice and hold the button down,  you can enter fredrive mode and manually move the arm to a desired position while the buttons light pressure is held down.
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons are a three-position enabling device on the Teach Pendant that control robot motion in Manual mode: [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

- Release (no pressure): robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (power retained, brakes released).  
- Light-press (middle position): allows a program to play/run when the robot is in Manual mode.  
- Tight-press (fully pressed): stops robot movement in Manual mode and places the robot in 3PE Stop.  

Additional notes: the 3PE buttons are only active in Manual mode; they are used for Freedrive and Backdrive sequences (specific press/release patterns are required to enter Freedrive/Backdrive). QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- Emergency Stop (E-stop) has been activated and latched. You must reset the E-stop after visually verifying the reason for the stop. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Recovery Mode was automatically activated because a safety limit was exceeded. In Recovery Mode, the robot can move within joint limits using Freedrive or Move tab, but you cannot run programs until the issue is resolved. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

How to check and respond:
- Check Teach Pendant for an active E-stop, then reset the E-stop as described. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- If no E-stop, verify whether Recovery Mode is active and move the arm back within limits using Freedrive/Move tab, then address the safety-limit cause. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Preventive actions:
- Ensure proper safety configuration settings are in place (speed limits, momentum limits, force limits, etc.) per the risk assessment to reduce inadvertent stops or unexpected movements. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Perform a thorough risk assessment before powered-on operation and configure safeguards accordingly (password protection, safeguarding, and appropriate emergency stops). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: - The 3PE buttons provide manual control in Manual mode. 
  - Position 1 (Release): no pressure; robot movement is stopped, brakes remain released, power not removed.
  - Position 2 (Light-press): some pressure; allows program to play when in Manual mode.
  - Position 3 (Tight-press): full pressure; robot movement is stopped (3PE Stop).

- In addition, 3PE can be used to operate program flow and special modes:
  - While in Manual, you can press and hold the 3PE button to play, stop, pause, or resume a program in PolyScope.
  - The 3PE can also be used to freedrive the arm or move the robot into the start position as described in the 8.5.3 “Using the 3PE Buttons” section. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reasons your UR5e arm looks or feels like it’s vibrating:

- Normal startup behavior: during power-up and when brakes are released, the robot arm may vibrate or rattle as the joints unlock and the system initializes. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

- Stand and mounting resonance: if the stand isn’t sufficiently stiff or has resonant modes (your setup should have a minimum stand resonance frequency of 45 Hz), you can observe vibration or movement as the arm operates. Ensure the stand is dimensioned for the loads and has adequate static/dynamic stiffness. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- Aggressive accelerations or improper loads can cause dynamic effects: high accelerations or loads beyond what the stand or mounting can safely handle can lead to vibrations or protective stops. You can reduce this by lowering acceleration limits or revising the mounting to increase stiffness. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- An Emergency Stop or Safeguard Stop was activated, which stops all robot motion (Stop Category 1 or 2) and may be followed by a reset before resuming. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- A safety limit was violated (e.g., joint speed/position limits, stopping time/distance, or tool/end effector limits), which triggers Recovery mode and prevents running programs until the safety issue is resolved. When recovering, the arm can be moved manually within limits but is effectively in a restricted state. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]

How to prevent recurrences:
- Perform a proper risk assessment and configure safety parameters (Normal vs Reduced safety modes) to ensure limits match the application. Check and apply the Safety Configuration and Safety Checksum to verify the active settings. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-106.pdf]
- Ensure correct use of emergency/safety devices: know when and how to reset an E-stop, Safeguard Stop, and Three-Position Enabling Device (if installed). Confirm that mode switching (Automatic/Manual) and any 3PE devices are used as intended. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Verify that the Safe Home, I/O safety signals, and any Safety Planes or Limits are configured according to the risk assessment and that operators understand how to keep within those limits during operation. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf], [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp108-120.pdf]

If unsure which event occurred, check:
- The Safety Checksum in PolyScope to see if safety settings changed, and inspect Safety-related sections (Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop, Recovery) for recent activity. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot appears to be vibrating when running, it may be resonance between the robot and its stand (the stand’s eigenfrequency matching the robot motion frequency). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Insufficient static or dynamic stiffness of the stand can cause deflection or resonance — the stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz to avoid this. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Poor mounting (not properly secured or uneven surface) or a stand that transmits external vibrations can produce the same symptoms; ensure the arm is tightened and the stand is sturdy. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Approaching a singularity can also cause sudden or fast movements that may feel like vibration; avoid programming motions that produce singularity poses. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- Set Tool Force, Elbow Force, Tool Speed, Elbow Speed, Power and Momentum limits (and joint/position/orientation limits to avoid exposing sharp edges) via the Software Safety Limits (Robot Limits) screen. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- Use appropriate Stopping Time and Stopping Distance limits (these automatically affect maximum speed) so the robot stops before exceeding configured limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: Why do I need to set the center of gravity for the payload?
STUDENT ANSWER: Because the robot’s rated payload depends on the payload’s center of gravity (CoG) offset: the CoG determines how much mass the robot can handle at a given reach and affects stopping/acceleration behavior. The controller automatically adjusts accelerations when payload mass, center of gravity and inertia are configured correctly, and the robot’s capacity to accelerate can be reduced if the payload CoG exceeds the robot’s reach and payload. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Additional practical point: set CoG correctly before using Freedrive or running the robot—incorrect payload or mounting settings can cause unwanted motion or increased risk (configure and save installation settings). QUESTION: Are there risks associated with using 12V vs 24V?
STUDENT ANSWER: Yes. Programmer or wiring errors can cause the voltage to change from 12V to 24V, which can lead to fire damage to equipment — verify the use of 12V and proceed with caution [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

Additional relevant points:
- Tool I/O supply voltages and currents have strict limits (12V and 24V modes, peak/average currents, soft-start, no hot-plugging of large capacitive loads); exceeding these can cause permanent damage [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- Some tool signals and outputs are not over-voltage/current protected (e.g., tool digital outputs are not current-limited; analog inputs are not protected against overvoltage), so incorrect voltage selection or wiring can damage the robot or tool [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: The sudden strong movement may be caused by the robot approaching a singularity or by a restart/resumption after a safety stop (stopping motion or monitored-stop resume) where joints can exceed normal torques or speed limits reset. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Supporting details and prevention steps:
- Singularity: As the robot approaches a singularity it can resist motion and then move unpredictably or suddenly; avoid programming motions that produce singular poses. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Stopping/resume dynamics: During stopping motion (category 0,1,2) joints may exceed nominal torques and cause strong forces when motion resumes; also safety-mode changes (e.g., enabling device activation) can reset speed limits. Use correct safety configuration and be cautious when resuming from safety-rated monitored stops. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons are a Three-Position Enabling Device used to allow deliberate operator control in Manual Mode: the device must be pressed and held in the center (on) position to permit robot movement (i.e., to move, program, or enable Freedrive/Backdrive) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

Supporting details:
- In Manual Mode, movement requires the 3PE to be pressed and held center-on; if a built‑in 3PE is used the mid position must be held to move the robot [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
- The 3PE is used to enable Backdrive and Freedrive sequences (e.g., 3PE Teach Pendant or external 3PE device must be operated to enter Backdrive) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
- A 3PE is recommended for programming and, when configured, causes the robot to operate at Manual Reduced Speed unless High Speed Manual Mode is explicitly activated [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]; see also comparison of 3PE behavior in safety I/O descriptions [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf].

QUESTION: How can I reduce the force applied to the operator in case of a collision?
STUDENT ANSWER: Set and use the robot’s safety functions to limit the robot’s energy transfer (force, momentum, speed) so collisions do not cause injury.

Supporting actions:
- Use Force and Power Limiting (PFL) to limit clamping forces and energy transfer on contact. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]
- Use Momentum Limiting to reduce transient impact energy (reduce speed/mass momenta). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why do I need to set the center of gravity for the payload?
STUDENT ANSWER: Because the robot’s rated payload depends on the payload center of gravity (CoG) offset — the distance from the tool flange to the payload CoG — you must set it so the controller can correctly assess capacity and motion. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Supporting points:

- Use URSim to evaluate accelerations and cycle times for a specific payload. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

QUESTION: What happens if I offset the center of gravity?
STUDENT ANSWER: The center of gravity (CoG) offset changes the rated payload and the robot’s dynamic performance: a larger CoG offset reduces the effective payload capacity and can reduce the robot’s ability to accelerate. Configure payload mass, center of gravity and inertia in the controller so the software automatically adjusts accelerations. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Likely causes: the robot approaching a singularity (causing sudden, fast/resisted motion) or abrupt stop/resume dynamics where joint torques/loads exceed normal values during stopping and restarting. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

How to prevent it:
- Avoid poses that can cause singularities and do not program motions that approach them. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Reduce joint accelerations/speeds in the program to lower operating loads and the forces during stops. (Normal operating loads can be reduced by lowering acceleration limits.) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Ensure the robot is mounted to a sufficiently stiff, vibration‑free stand (minimize deflection/resonance and follow the recommended stiffness/resonance guidance), and verify mounting bolts/torque. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  

If you need more specific diagnostics (e.g., logs, safety events, or program node where it happened), provide those and I will point to relevant checks in the manual.

- Note: hot‑plugging large capacitive loads is not allowed and tool power is turned off after an Emergency Stop — ensure these conditions are not preventing operation [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE (Three-Position Enabling) buttons are an enabling device that must be pressed and held in the center-on position to allow robot movement in Manual Mode; they do not affect Automatic Mode. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Supporting details:
- When a Three-Position Enabling Device is used and the robot is in Manual Mode, movement requires the device to be held in the center-on position; if released the robot performs a Safeguard Stop (or will not move) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- A 3PE Teach Pendant is recommended for programming; if other persons may be inside the safeguarded space in Manual Mode, additional 3PE devices can be integrated and configured [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- The 3PE input is a permanent safety input (Category 3, PLd) and is intended for use with enabling devices per the safety I/O description [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- A safety stop occurred (safety-rated monitored stop or a protective stop) which momentarily held the robot and then released, causing a strong movement when re-enabled or when limits were cleared. This is described as a safety function in UR e-Series systems. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]
- The robot transitioned from teach/program mode or used an enabling device (3-position enabling device) which can impose a temporary speed/limit change and then allow a rapid move when released. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]
- A singularity or near-singularity condition which can cause resisted or abrupt movements as the arm approaches a singular pose. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] Note: avoid moves that approach singularities. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

How to prevent reoccurrence (concise guidance):
- Ensure proper use of safety features: operate in the intended mode (Manual vs Automatic) and use a compliant enabling device (e.g., 3-position enabling device) when required. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]
- Avoid poses that can cause singularities; plan moves to stay clear of singular configurations. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Verify Safety and Mode settings after any fault: check that safety stops are cleared only through proper procedures and that the robot is in the correct mode before resuming operation. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

If you want, I can help you review your current mode, safety device status, and any recent camera/log events to pinpoint the exact trigger. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes
- A stopping-performance event where the robot stopped and then resumed with momentum, e.g., stopping/stopping-limit settings or a restart after a stop or power interruption causing a sudden movement. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Incorrect or changed safety-configuration parameters (including stopping time/distance limits, momentum, force/power or speed limits). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Items or tooling released or moved after a power interruption, or unexpected motion because a hazardous tool/end effector is not properly safeguarded. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to prevent it happening again
- Perform and document an application risk assessment (integrator’s responsibility) and verify safety configuration settings before powering the application for the first time. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Enable and set password protection for safety configuration to prevent unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Configure appropriate safety functions: use stopping time limit or stopping distance limit (these automatically affect speed and remove the need for manual periodic stopping tests), and enable momentum, force/power and speed limiting as needed for your application. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- If hazards cannot be eliminated by built-in functions (e.g., hazardous tool/process), add external safeguarding per ISO 10218-2. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If you need, I can list which safety settings to check and where to find them in the robot’s configuration.

STUDENT ANSWER: Yes.

- Stop Category 0: Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

- Stop Category 2: Stop the robot while keeping power available to the drives, maintaining the trajectory; drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3-Position Enabling (3PE) buttons control manual enabling of robot motion and have three positions:

- Release (no pressure): robot movement is stopped in Manual mode; power remains and brakes stay released.  
- Light-press (middle): allows a program to play in Manual mode (used to run, resume, freedrive, and Automove into start position).  
- Tight-press (full): robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (robot is in 3PE Stop).

The 3PE buttons are only active in Manual mode and are also used for Freedrive and Move Robot into Position operations. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the application risk assessment guidance)
- Incorrect safety configuration or unauthorized changes to safety parameters (can cause unexpected behaviour) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Confusion or incorrect wiring/understanding of multiple emergency stops or stops/modes (mistaken understanding of what is controlled by multiple E‑stops) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Faulty or loose mechanical parts (loose bolts) or items moving/falling from the end effector after a stop or power interruption, producing a sudden movement or impact [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Stopping/performance behaviour if limits are not set appropriately (stopping time/distance settings affect speed and stopping; incorrect use or configuration can lead to unexpected motion) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

How to prevent it
- Perform and document an application risk assessment before first power‑on and iteratively after installation, covering teaching, troubleshooting, maintenance and normal operation [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Set and protect safety configuration passwords so only authorized, competent persons can change settings; implement a password management program [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Verify safety configuration settings (including stopping time and stopping distance limits) and ensure they match the assessed risks; use these built‑in functions to limit speed, momentum and force where appropriate [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Physically verify connections and mechanical security (tighten bolts, secure the tool/end effector and payload) after installation [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Add safeguarding if hazards cannot be eliminated by built‑in safety functions (e.g., hazardous tools/processes) per ISO 10218‑2 [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Remove obstacles and/or use joint, elbow, tool position limits and safety planes to eliminate pinch or collision areas in the workspace [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  

If you need, run through your current safety configuration, stopping limits, E‑stop wiring/behaviour and mechanical checks and I can point to which settings to review.

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible cause:
- The robot’s safety configuration may have activated stopping performance limits (Stopping Time Limit or Stopping Distance Limit) or other safety functions (momentum limiting, force/power limiting, or speed limitation), causing a strong, sudden stop or quick retraction.

How to prevent:
- Ensure proper safety configuration settings are in place and protected (enable password protection and manage access) before operation. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Conduct an application risk assessment and configure energy transfer and motion limits (force/power, momentum, speed, and orientation/position limits) according to the task and hazards. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- If hazards cannot be sufficiently mitigated, implement safeguarding per ISO 10218-2. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons are active only in Manual mode and have three positions:

- Position 3 (Tight-press): Robot movement is stopped in Manual mode; the robot is in 3PE Stop.

QUESTION: How can I reduce the force applied to the operator in case of a collision?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use the robot’s safety configuration to apply force-, momentum- and speed-limiting functions so that energy transfer in a collision is reduced. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Supporting options (configure via Safety Configuration):
- Force and power limiting: reduce clamping forces and pressures exerted by robot, end-effector and workpiece during collisions. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Momentum limiting: reduce transient energy/impact forces by lowering robot speed to limit momentum. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Speed limitation: ensure robot speed stays below configured limits to reduce impact energy. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Stopping Time/Stopping Distance limits: tighten these to reduce stopping time/distance so the robot stops sooner, reducing force transferred. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Joint/elbow/tool position and tool orientation limiting: avoid movements or exposures that increase risk (e.g., point sharp edges away from operator) which can reduce injury severity in contact. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Also ensure these settings are defined as part of the application risk assessment and protected from unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes
- Enabling Freedrive while the robot was being pushed or touched, which can cause drift leading to faults and unexpected/sudden motion when brakes or control state change [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Unexpected start-up or release of brakes (e.g., powering on or pressing START) causing the arm to move as brakes are released [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Incorrect payload or installation settings (or a payload mismatch) causing control/sensor behavior that can produce unexpected movement [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Unauthorized or incorrect changes to safety configuration or missing password protection, allowing settings that affect stopping or motion to be changed [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Loose bolts, poorly attached tooling, or items falling from the end effector that change dynamics and produce sudden motion or impacts [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

How to prevent it (short actions)
- Do not enable Freedrive while you are pushing or touching the robot; enable Freedrive only when intentionally setting positions [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Verify actual payload and installation settings before powering up or releasing brakes, and ensure the correct tool is securely attached [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Always power down the robot before mounting/dismounting to avoid unexpected start-up; unplug mains and wait 30 seconds to discharge stored energy [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Conduct an application risk assessment and set/maintain password protection for safety configuration so unauthorized changes cannot be made [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Check mechanical fastening (bolts, tool mounting) and secure the end effector to avoid items falling or changing dynamic behavior [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  

If you need, I can list specific safety-configuration settings (e.g., stopping time/distance, force/momentum limits) to apply for your application.

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
STUDENT ANSWER: There are three stop categories defined (per IEC 60204-1):

- Stop Category 0 — stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 1 — stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 2 — stop the robot while maintaining drive power; drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. Universal Robots’ Category 2 stops are further described as SS1 or SS2 according to IEC 61800-5-2. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Typical safety triggers and their stop-category reactions:
- Emergency Stop → Stop Category 1.  
- Safeguard Stop → Stop Category 2.  
- Limit violation or fault detection → Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: There are three kinds of stop categories.
Stop Category 0: Immediately stops the arm by removing the power.
Stop Category 1: Stops the robot in a controlled manner, and removes the power once it is fully stopped.
Stop Category 2: Stops the robot with power available to the drives, while maintaining the current trajectory. Power is maintained after the robot is stopped.
STUDENT ANSWER: There are three stop categories defined (per IEC 60204-1):

- Stop Category 0 — stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 1 — stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 2 — stop the robot while maintaining drive power; drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. Universal Robots’ Category 2 stops are further described as SS1 or SS2 according to IEC 61800-5-2. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Typical safety triggers and their stop-category reactions:
- Emergency Stop → Stop Category 1.  
- Safeguard Stop → Stop Category 2.  
- Limit violation or fault detection → Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- Incorrect or unauthenticated changes to safety configuration parameters, leading to unexpected motions (risk assessment section emphasizes correct safety settings and password protection) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
- Freedrive being enabled during movement, which can cause the arm to drift or move unexpectedly if the button/mode is activated incorrectly [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].
- Activation near joint limits or singularities, which can feel like a strong, sudden movement as resistance increases in Freedrive mode [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].
- Hitting stopping performance limits (stopping time/distance limits) or other safety settings that automatically adjust speed or cause a stop, leading to abrupt motion if configured or triggered [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

How to prevent:
- Always conduct an application risk assessment and enable password protection for safety configuration to limit unauthorized changes [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
- Verify payload and installation settings before starting the robot, and ensure they match the actual setup [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].
- Avoid enabling Freedrive while the robot is moving, and use Freedrive only with proper precautions (or during planned, controlled positioning) [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].
- Review and configure stopping time and stopping distance limits so stopping behavior is predictable, with continuous safety control active [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the manuals)
- Unexpected release of brakes/start-up motion when the robot was powered on or START was pressed (Freedrive/backdrive behavior or normal brake release during start-up). [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Enabling Freedrive while the arm was being pushed or touched, causing drift or sudden motion. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Incorrect or missing safety configuration (stopping time/distance limits, speed/force/momentum limits), or unauthorized changes to those settings. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Incorrect payload or installation settings (affecting braking/drive behavior). [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Loose bolts, poor tool/end effector mounting, or items flying from the end effector causing abrupt movements. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Singularity or approach to joint limits which can change resistance and cause abrupt motion when escaping the condition. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

How to prevent it (concise actions)
- Perform and document a full application risk assessment before operation and after installation, addressing stopping performance and collision risks. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Verify and set correct payload, mounting and installation settings before use; confirm all bolts and tool/end effector attachments are secure. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf][003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Configure appropriate safety settings (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, stopping time/distance limits) and enable password protection to prevent unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Avoid enabling Freedrive while pushing or touching the robot; use the documented Freedrive procedures and Backdrive if you need to move joints without releasing all brakes. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Inform users of emergency stop locations and ensure emergency stops and any additional safeguarding are installed if built-in functions are insufficient. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf][004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
STUDENT ANSWER: There are three stop categories defined (IEC 60204-1):

- Stop Category 0 — Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 1 — Stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]  
- Stop Category 2 — Stop the robot while keeping drive power available, maintaining the trajectory; drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. (UR robots’ Category 2 stops are further classified as SS1 or SS2 per IEC 61800-5-2.) [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Additional relevant points:
- Emergency Stop and Robot Emergency Stop trigger Stop Category 1; Safeguard Stop triggers Stop Category 2; limit violations or safety faults trigger Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Likely causes: minor vibrations when joint brakes are released during startup, or resonance/insufficient stiffness of the mounting/stand. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf] [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:
- During initialization you may hear/see minor vibrations as joint brakes are released; use Backdrive if vibrations are undesirable near a collision [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].

- Also verify the robot is not near a singularity or incorrectly mounted, as singularities and incorrect mounting can cause abrupt motion or perceived vibration [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: How can I reduce the force applied to the operator in case of a collision?
STUDENT ANSWER: Direct answer:
Use the robot’s safety functions to limit energy transfer—primarily the Force Limit (and/or Power Limit and Momentum Limit), plus Speed Limit, Safety Planes, joint/pose and Tool Orientation limits; configure these in the Safety Configuration to reduce forces in collisions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Force and power limiting: set the Force Limit (and Power Limit) to cap the maximum force/power at the tool, elbow and defined TCP positions. These functions are intended to reduce clamping pressures in collisions. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Momentum and speed: use Momentum Limit and Speed Limit to reduce transient impact energy and maximum speed, respectively. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Geometry and orientation controls: use Safety Planes, Joint Position Limits and Tool Orientation limits to prevent motion toward sensitive body areas or to keep sharp edges/protrusions turned inward. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Reduced Mode and dynamic changes: you can configure Normal and Reduced parameter sets (triggered by planes or inputs) so the robot uses lower limits when an operator is nearby. Validate timing (≤500 ms) and the 20 mm plane transition area. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]  
- Do a documented application risk assessment and verify/validate all safety parameter values for the specific end-effector, workpiece and tasks; unauthorized changes must be prevented (password protection). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Are there risks associated with using 12V vs 24V?
STUDENT ANSWER: Yes. The documentation identifies several risks when using 12V vs 24V:

- Programmer or wiring errors can cause the voltage to change from 12V to 24V and lead to fire damage to equipment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Tool I/O limitations and cautions:
  - Tool supply voltages and currents differ between 12V and 24V modes; exceeding specified currents or duty cycles can damage the tool (see peak and average current limits, and recommended protective diode for inductive loads). Hot‑plugging large capacitive loads is not allowed. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]
  - Digital outputs in the tool are not current‑limited; overriding specs can cause permanent damage. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]
  - Analog inputs are not protected against over‑voltage in current mode; exceeding specs can cause permanent damage. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]
- Operational effects:
  - After an Emergency Stop the tool power pins are set to 0V (power off). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]
- General wiring and safety advice:
  - Verify use of 12V and proceed with caution (to avoid incorrect voltages). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
  - Follow all electrical specifications and warnings when connecting I/O and tools. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]

If you need specific limits or wiring guidance for a particular tool or signal, tell me which I/O or connector and I will quote the exact specification.

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the manual)
- Brakes released during start/initialization: starting the robot releases joint brakes and is accompanied by sound and slight movements when brakes are released [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Freedrive / Backdrive enabled: enabling Freedrive or Backdrive lets joints move with little resistance or heavy-to-move backdrive and can result in unexpected motion if engaged accidentally [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf; 003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].  
- Emergency stop reset or mode changes: resetting an E‑stop or switching modes (Manual/Automatic/Recovery) can restore drive power and allow motion; Recovery Mode disables some limits and allows movement to be performed to bring the arm within joint limits [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- Stopping/stop-performance settings or incorrect safety configuration: incorrect safety configuration parameters or removed protections (including unauthorized changes) can cause unexpected starts or sudden motions; insufficient safeguarding when hazards can’t be eliminated is a risk [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].  
- Forced back-driving / movement without drive power: forced back-driving (manual moving when power is off) can require high force and cause sudden movement if not controlled and may need more than one person [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  

How to prevent it happening again (actions to take)
- Perform and follow the application risk assessment and set the safety configuration accordingly (including Stopping Time/Stopping Distance limits if appropriate) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Always verify payload and installation before powering or starting the arm, and follow the proper start/shutdown procedure to avoid unintended brake release or initialization motion [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- Enable password protection for safety configuration to prevent unauthorized changes and maintain a password management program so only trained personnel change settings [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Use emergency stops and any additional E‑stop devices required by the risk assessment; after an E‑stop, visually inspect and resolve the cause before resetting and restoring power [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- Avoid enabling Freedrive/Backdrive unless intentionally positioning or servicing the robot; do not enable Freedrive while pushing/touching the robot [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf].  
- If Recovery Mode was involved, move the arm back cautiously (use Freedrive or Move tab) because some safety limits are disabled during Recovery Mode [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].  
- Inform and train personnel about emergency procedures, mode switching, location/function of E‑stops, and risks of unexpected motion [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].  

If you need, tell me what happened step-by-step (power state, whether E‑stop was pressed/reset, if Freedrive/Backdrive was active) and I can point to the most likely single cause and the specific setting to check.

STUDENT ANSWER: Stop Category 0: Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Stop Category 1: Stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Stop Category 2: Stop the robot while keeping drive power available (drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped). Universal Robots’ Category 2 stops are further described as SS1 or SS2 type stops according to IEC 61800-5-2. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes:
- The robot entered Recovery Mode or was forced to move manually due to safety limits being exceeded. Recovery Mode is a manual-mode state activated when a safety limit is violated, and it can produce controlled but abrupt movement as the arm is brought back within limits. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- An emergency stop (E-stop) was actuated, which stops all motion with Stop Category 1, and may be reset only after assessing the situation. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Safety configuration parameters (e.g., momentum, speed, or position/orientation limits) or incorrect/unauthorized changes to safety settings could cause unexpected stopping or sudden motion when the limits are reached or re-engaged. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

What you should do to diagnose now:
- Check whether the E-stop has been actuated and reset it properly after a visual assessment of the situation. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Review the safety configuration settings (speed, momentum, force/power limits, position/orientation limits) and ensure they match the risk assessment for your application. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Verify the current operational mode (Automatic/Manual/Freedrive/Recovery) and confirm that no mode intended for programming or manual positioning is active if not desired. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

How to prevent recurrence:
- Perform an application risk assessment and ensure the safety configuration settings are properly set and protected (password protection). This includes confirming momentum limiting, speed limiting, and joint/tool limits are appropriate for the task. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Ensure safeguarding is in place for any hazards that cannot be eliminated by the built-in safety functions, and keep the robot within the verified safeguarded space when applicable. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Verify payload and installation are correct before operation, and maintain correct mode usage (e.g., use Manual/Automatic modes as appropriate, with Freedrive disabled when not needed). [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf], [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Notes:
- If a recovery or E-stop event occurred, always visually inspect the system and assess the reason before resuming. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer:
After modifying the robot arm you must perform safety and functional checks to ensure required safety level and correct operation of all safety functions, and conduct the commissioning tests listed for first use or after modifications. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf] [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Supporting checks (from the sources):
- Perform post-maintenance checks to ensure required safety level and that all safety functions operate correctly; follow applicable national/regional work safety regulations. Also verify earth connection before re-powering and observe ESD and contamination precautions. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Commissioning tests to run after modifications:
  - Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - Test all connected safety inputs/outputs (including devices common to multiple machines) function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - Test Emergency Stop buttons/inputs to verify the robot stops and brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

  - Change operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - Test the 3-position enabling device (center position enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed). [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the E‑Stop push-button and verify whole-system stop. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - Test system outputs tied to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, Not Reduced Mode to verify output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
  - Determine and fulfill any additional commissioning requirements specific to your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Unplug the main power and make the system safe before beginning maintenance.  
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources; take precautions to prevent others from powering the system during repairs. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Additional essential precautions:  
- Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]  
- Observe ESD regulations when disassembling parts of the robot arm or Control Box, and prevent water and dust ingress. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]  
- Avoid disassembling the Control Box power supply too soon after switching off because high voltages (up to 600 V) can remain for several hours. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]  
- Only perform maintenance, inspection, calibration and repair work according to the latest Service Manual; repair work should be done by Universal Robots or client-designated trained individuals following the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Follow general safety practices before and during maintenance (verify secure mounting, protect personnel, and be aware of hot surfaces and pinch hazards). [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the tool attachments I can put on the universal robot relating to moving objects with the arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You attach an end effector (also called the tool or workpiece) to the robot’s tool flange to let the arm manipulate or move objects [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf].

Common types of tool attachments for moving objects mentioned in the manual:
- Grippers (mechanical/robotic grippers) for picking and placing parts.  
- General-purpose tools used for manipulating workpieces (examples given: QC inspection tools, adhesive dispensers, welding tools) — note grippers and sensors use the tool connector for power/control [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf; 008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

Key integration points and requirements:
- Mount to the tool output flange (ISO 9409‑1) and follow the flange dimensions and mounting rules (use radially slotted hole for positioning pin; bolts must not extend beyond 10 mm) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- Use the Tool Connector (8‑pin) for grippers and sensors; observe pin functions, tighten connector to max 0.4 Nm, and follow Tool I/O voltage/current settings and mode (0V/12V/24V, single/dual pin, DO/DI modes) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- If required, use the Tool Cable Adapter and follow the safety warning to connect the adapter to the tool before connecting to a powered robot [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

If you need specifics (recommended gripper models, mounting drawings, wiring examples), consult the end effector’s documentation and the Tool I/O installation/spec sections referenced above [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What are the tool attachments I can put on the universal robot relating to moving objects with the arm?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Many kinds of grippers such as parallel, three-finger, vacuum, magnetic, soft, and precision grippers.
STUDENT ANSWER: You attach an end effector (also called the tool or workpiece) to the robot’s tool flange to let the arm manipulate or move objects [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf].

Common types of tool attachments for moving objects mentioned in the manual:
- Grippers (mechanical/robotic grippers) for picking and placing parts.  
- General-purpose tools used for manipulating workpieces (examples given: QC inspection tools, adhesive dispensers, welding tools) — note grippers and sensors use the tool connector for power/control [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf; 008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

Key integration points and requirements:
- Mount to the tool output flange (ISO 9409‑1) and follow the flange dimensions and mounting rules (use radially slotted hole for positioning pin; bolts must not extend beyond 10 mm) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- Use the Tool Connector (8‑pin) for grippers and sensors; observe pin functions, tighten connector to max 0.4 Nm, and follow Tool I/O voltage/current settings and mode (0V/12V/24V, single/dual pin, DO/DI modes) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- If required, use the Tool Cable Adapter and follow the safety warning to connect the adapter to the tool before connecting to a powered robot [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

If you need specifics (recommended gripper models, mounting drawings, wiring examples), consult the end effector’s documentation and the Tool I/O installation/spec sections referenced above [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced mode is a safety mode that applies a more restrictive set of safety limits than Normal mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

Supporting details:
- Reduced mode becomes active when the robot Tool Center Point (TCP) is positioned beyond a Trigger Reduced mode plane or when it is triggered using a configurable safety input. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- You can configure separate safety limits for Normal and Reduced; Reduced limits for tool and joints must be more restrictive than Normal. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- When switching due to a safety input, up to 500 ms can elapse before the new (Reduced or Normal) limits become active. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
