QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is a workspace area where a person can be pinched between moving parts of the robot (arm, wrist, elbow) and nearby obstacles or the robot structure, which can lead to injury. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to avoid pinch hazards (brief):
- Remove obstacles or reposition the robot to eliminate the hazardous areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use safety planes and joint limits to prevent the robot from moving into pinching areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Be aware of specific pinch-risk zones noted by Universal Robots (e.g., radial motions when wrist‑1 is a given distance from the base and areas within ~200 mm of the base when moving tangentially). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: Risk: Very high electromagnetic signal levels or excessive EMC exposure can cause unexpected behaviors, permanent damage to the robot, and EMC-related error messages in the log (EMC problems are often seen in welding processes). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]

How to avoid it:
- Keep interfering signal levels within the international IEC standards used to test the robot. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Avoid placing the robot where strong EMC sources exist (e.g., welding) or perform additional testing if such processes are required. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Follow installation best practices: use only the original supplied cables, ensure proper grounding (PE via M6 screw earth connections), keep I/O cable runs from the Control Box to other equipment ≤ 30 m unless additional tests are performed, and remove metal shavings when drilling cable-entry plates. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Unplug the main power and make the system safe.
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources; take precautions to prevent others from powering the system during repairs. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Verify grounding and electrical hazards.
- Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Avoid disassembling the Control Box power supply soon after switch-off—high voltages (up to 600 V) can remain for several hours. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Prevent mechanical hazards when removing power.
- Support the robot arm before removing power to avoid the arm breaking or falling. Do not move joints more than necessary (and no joint >160°) when manually moving the arm. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]  
- Forced back‑driving or manual movement requires high force and may need two or more people. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Protect parts and personnel during disassembly.
- Observe ESD regulations when parts of the robot arm or Control Box are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Use trained personnel and correct procedures.
- Conduct maintenance, inspection, calibration and repair according to the latest Service Manual; repair should be done by Universal Robots or client‑designated trained individuals following the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Perform all inspections and tests required to ensure the required safety level and verify correct functioning of all safety functions after maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Additional general precautions.
- Read and follow the general safety warnings (securely bolt arm and tools, avoid loose clothing/jewelry, inform users of emergency stop locations, perform a risk assessment). [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the tool attachments I can put on the universal robot relating to moving objects with the arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can attach end effectors (tools) such as grippers and other tooling for moving objects; these mount to the robot Tool Flange (ISO 9409‑1) and may include sensors or actuators (e.g., grippers for pick‑and‑place, inspection tools, dispensers) [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf].

Key integration points and requirements:
- Mounting: tools bolt to the tool output flange (ISO 9409‑1); use radially slotted hole for a positioning pin, do not use bolts that extend beyond 10 mm, and ensure bolts are tightened properly to avoid dropping the tool [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Tool Connector / Tool I/O: an 8‑pin tool connector at Wrist 3 provides power and signals for grippers/sensors (pins include analog inputs, digital inputs/outputs, POWER, GND, RS485) and the connector must be tightened to max 0.4 Nm [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Tool Cable Adapter / hot‑plugging: use the Tool Cable Adapter when required and connect the adapter to the tool before connecting to the robot; do not connect the adapter to the robot while powered on [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Power and I/O capabilities: tool power can be set to 0V/12V/24V; supply current, peak limits, and soft‑start/capacitive load limits apply (see Tool I/O installation specs); tool digital outputs support sinking, sourcing or push/pull modes; analog and digital I/O are available for sensors/actuators [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Robot configuration: when adding a payload/gripper, define the Payload (mass, CoG, inertia) and use Set Payload or the Payload Estimation Wizard so the controller adjusts accelerations and avoids robot stops; switch payloads in program where appropriate (e.g., after gripper closes) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf].

If you need exact pinouts, power limits, or mounting dimensions, refer to the Tool I/O and Tool Flange sections for full electrical and mechanical specifications [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf] and mounting/payload guidance [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part01.pdf].

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety system state in which a separate set of more restrictive safety limits (the Reduced parameter set) is active instead of the Normal limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

When Reduced Mode is used:
- It is activated automatically when the robot Tool Center Point (TCP) or elbow crosses a configured Trigger Reduced Mode plane, or when triggered by a configured safety input (e.g., a safety I/O). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]  
- It can also be initiated externally via safety inputs (the transition may take up to 500 ms to reach the new limits). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- While in Reduced Mode, the Reduced-mode limits (e.g., joint speed, TCP speed, force, momentum, stopping time/distance) are applied and must be more restrictive than Normal mode for tool and joint limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is an area of the robot workspace where parts of the robot can pinch or crush a person’s body between moving robot parts or between the robot and nearby obstacles, which can lead to injury. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Supporting points:
- You can avoid pinch hazards by removing obstacles, repositioning the robot, or using safety planes and joint limits to prevent the robot from moving into those areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Notable pinch-hazard areas: radial motions when wrist 1 is at least 750 mm from the base, and within 200 mm of the base when moving tangentially. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: The risk: very high electromagnetic signal levels can cause unexpected behaviours or permanent damage to the robot (EMC problems are commonly found in welding processes and are normally indicated by error messages in the log). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]

How to avoid it:
- Do not expose the robot to signal levels above the applicable IEC EMC standards; avoid placing the robot near strong sources (e.g., welding equipment). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Keep I/O cable runs from the Control Box to other machinery ≤ 30 m unless you perform additional EMC tests. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Monitor the robot log for EMC-related error messages and investigate immediately; note Universal Robots cannot be held responsible for EMC-caused damage. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]

(Also avoid exposure to very strong magnetic fields, which can damage the robot.) [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Main safety precautions before maintenance:

- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box to ensure the system is completely unpowered, and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Check the earth/ground connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations and prevent water or dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Do not disassemble the power supply inside the Control Box and be aware that high voltages (up to 600 V) can be present for hours after shutdown. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Reduced Mode is a safety mode where safety limits are more restrictive than Normal mode. It is active when the tool/endpoint is in a reduced state.

- It is used when the robot moves beyond a Trigger Reduced plane or is externally triggered by a safety input (as defined in the Safety Parameter Sets). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__10.3.5._Software_SafetyModes__pp107-113.pdf] 
- Planes can trigger Reduced mode: a Trigger Reduced plane causes the system to switch to Reduced mode; safety planes can also be configured to enforce Normal, Reduced, or both depending on mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__10.4._Software_SafetyRestrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?

- How to avoid:
  - Keep I/O cables within length limits (not longer than 30 m unless extra tests are performed). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]
  - Ensure safety interface signals are kept separate from normal I/O signals. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]
  - Use only original cables supplied with the robot. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]

Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.

Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.

motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Main safety precautions before maintenance (UR5e):

- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box to ensure it is completely unpowered, and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box. Prevent others from powering on the system during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Check the earth connection before repowering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations when parts of the robot arm or Control Box are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Repairs should only be performed by Universal Robots; client-designated trained individuals may perform repair work only if they follow the Service Manual. See Chapter 5 for full inspection plan. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- After maintenance, verify safety by testing the correct functioning of all safety functions and ensure compliance with applicable safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- When handling grease or lubricants during maintenance, follow PPE and ventilation guidance (gloves, eye protection, avoid skin/eye contact, proper disposal). [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is a risk where the robot can pinch or trap body parts between moving parts or between the robot and obstacles. UR identifies pinching hazards and provides ways to avoid them, such as removing obstacles and using safety planes and joint limits.

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer:
After modifying the robot arm you must perform the required safety and functional checks described for maintenance and commissioning, including verifying safety inputs/outputs and testing emergency stops, safeguards, stopping performance and mechanical connections. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf] [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Supporting checklist (key actions from the sources):
- Ensure safe work practices before/after repair:
  - Unplug the main power cable from the Control Box and prevent others from powering the system.  
  - Check the earth connection before re-powering.  
  - Observe ESD regulations and prevent water/dust ingress. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Functional safety and commissioning tests (required after modifications):
  - Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected and functioning.  
  - Test emergency stop buttons/inputs to confirm the robot stops and brakes engage.  
  - Test safeguard inputs (and any safeguard reset) to confirm robot motion stops as intended.  
  - Test that operational mode changes and the 3-position enabling device behave as expected.  
  - If used, press Emergency Stop outputs and verify the whole system stops; test Robot Moving / Robot Not Stopping / Reduced Mode outputs if connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

- Mechanical and inspection checks (robot arm specific):
  - Move the Robot Arm to ZERO (if possible) and follow the Robot Arm Inspection Plan.  
  - Turn off and disconnect the Control Box power cable; inspect the cable between Control Box and Robot Arm for damage.  
  - Check base mounting bolts and tool flange bolts are properly tightened; inspect and replace worn flat rings.  
  - Perform the Freedrive inspection to verify the arm holds position without support and Freedrive is not active. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Stopping performance:
  - Test stopping performance periodically and after modifications to ensure stopping time/distance are acceptable; modify safeguarding if stopping performance is degraded. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?

- After maintenance, perform checks to ensure the required safety level and verify correct functioning of all safety functions in accordance with national/regional work safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Observe ESD regulations when parts are disassembled, and prevent water and dust ingress into the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Do not disassemble the Control Box power supply too quickly after switching off (high voltages up to 600 V may be present for several hours). [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Perform a risk assessment and ensure safety configuration settings (including password protection for safety configuration) are managed so unauthorized changes cannot occur. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform safety, functional and inspection checks after modifying the robot arm.

Direct actions (safety and power) — do these before/after work
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources; prevent others from re-powering the system during repair.  
- Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering.  
- Observe ESD rules when disassembling parts and prevent water/dust ingress.  
- Perform post-maintenance checks to ensure the required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions in accordance with local regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Commissioning and functional tests (required after modifications)
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to other machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended.  
- Test all Emergency Stop buttons/inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if Safeguard Reset is configured, verify it functions.  
- Activate the initialization screen reduced input and verify the screen changes.  
- Change operational mode and verify the mode icon updates in PolyScope.  
- Test the Three-Position Enabling Device (3PE) to verify center-on enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.  
- If Emergency Stop outputs or other safety outputs are used, press the E-stop and verify the system outputs change as expected (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced/Not Reduced etc.).  
- Determine and perform any additional commissioning requirements for your specific application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Additional notes
- After maintenance/repair, checks must adhere to valid national/regional work safety regulations and the Service Manual; repair work should follow the latest Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the tool attachments I can put on the universal robot relating to moving objects with the arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can attach end effectors (tools) such as grippers and other tooling for manipulating workpieces — examples given include grippers, QC/inspection tools, gluing/dispensing tools and welding tools. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Relevant integration and connection options/specs:
- The tool is mounted to the tool output flange (ISO 9409-1) on Wrist 3; use a radially slotted hole for the positioning pin and do not use bolts that extend beyond 10 mm. Ensure bolts are tightened properly to avoid dropping the tool [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- The tool connector (eight‑pin) provides power and control signals for grippers and sensors; pin functions are listed (analog/RS485, digital inputs TI0/TI1, digital outputs TO0/TO1, POWER, GND). The tool connector must be manually tightened up to 0.4 Nm [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- A Tool Cable Adapter is available to interface some tools; connect the adapter to the tool before connecting it to a powered robot (hot‑plug warning) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Tool I/O power can be set to 0V/12V/24V in the Installation Tab; electrical limits, single/dual pin power modes, peak/average currents and soft‑start/capacitive load restrictions are specified (see Tool I/O Installation Specifications and Tool Power Supply) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Tool digital I/O modes (sinking/sourcing/push‑pull) and their electrical characteristics are configurable in the Installation Tab; note Digital Outputs are deactivated after an Emergency Stop [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

NOTICE/CAUTION highlights:
- Refer to the specific end effector/tool documentation for mounting and connection details (UR provides such documentation) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Do not connect the Tool Cable Adapter to the robot while the robot is powered; connect adapter to the tool first [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Very long M8 bolts can short the tool flange — do not use bolts >10 mm [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

If you need examples or recommended UR+ grippers/accessories, refer to UR+ and the specific end‑effector documentation (see links in 002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf).

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety system state in which a separate, more restrictive set of safety limits (e.g., joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed/force, momentum, power, stopping time/distance) is active instead of the Normal limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

When it is used
- It is activated automatically when the robot Tool Center Point (TCP) or elbow passes a configured Trigger Reduced Mode plane (a 20 mm transition area around the plane is allowed) [010__L1__10...10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf; 010__L1__10...10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- It can also be triggered by a configured safety input; when triggered by an input, the robot adapts to the Reduced limits within up to 500 ms [010__L1__10...10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10...10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- Reduced Mode is a state change (not a separate safety function) that makes all Reduced-mode limit parameters active for risk-reduction purposes [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf; 010__L1__10...10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is a workspace area where the robot arm can trap or pinch a person between moving parts (robot, end effector or nearby obstacles), creating a risk of injury. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Such hazards can be avoided by removing nearby obstacles, repositioning the robot, or preventing motion into the area using safety planes and joint limits. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

[004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to avoid it:

- Avoid high-EMC processes (e.g., welding) near the robot or perform additional EMC testing if such processes are required. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Keep I/O cable runs from the Control Box to other machinery ≤ 30 m unless additional tests are performed. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Design the installation per relevant EMC standards (e.g., IEC 61000‑6‑4 industrial location) and follow best practices for cable routing and grounding. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Before performing maintenance on a UR5e arm, follow these main safety precautions:

- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box; ensure others cannot power it back on during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Check the earth connection before re-powering and observe ESD regulations when parts of the robot arm or Control Box are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Do not disassemble the power supply inside the Control Box too quickly after switching off; high voltages (up to 600 V) can be present for hours after shutdown. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: - EMC interference can cause damaging or unpredictable robot behavior if subjected to very high signal levels or excessive exposure. The robot has been tested to IEC EMC standards, and problems are often seen in welding environments. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]

- How to avoid it:
  - Keep signals within the IEC standards and design the interface signals with proper separation between safety and normal I/O signals. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]
  - Use the original cables and avoid exposing I/O cables to excessive flexing; ensure I/O cables between the Control Box and other equipment are not longer than 30 meters unless tested. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety-parameter set (a state change) in which all reduced-mode limits are active for the robot’s safety functions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Supporting details:
- Reduced Mode is not itself a safety function but a state that changes the limits for joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time and stopping distance. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- It can be initiated by a Trigger Reduced safety plane (behavior starts at 2 cm from the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm) or by an external safety input; when initiated by an input, the robot adapts to the new limits within up to 500 ms. Reduced Mode is also active when configured external connections are Low. QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform commissioning checks and safety verifications after any modification to the robot arm.

Required checks (concise list)
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test Emergency Stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage; if Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops, and if a safeguard reset is configured, verify it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Verify initialization and mode indications: inspect the initialization screen (activate reduced input to confirm screen changes) and change operational mode to verify the mode icon updates on PolyScope. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test the 3‑position enabling device: press to center position to verify motion enable in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test any system outputs you use (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, Not Reduced Mode) to verify the outputs change as expected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Determine and fulfil any additional commissioning requirements specific to your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Safety and procedural reminders
- After maintenance/repair, perform checks to ensure the required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions, in accordance with national/regional work safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Follow safety precautions when working on the arm or Control Box (disconnect main power, prevent re-powering, check earth connection before re-powering, observe ESD rules, prevent water/dust ingress). [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Unplug and lock out power: unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources; take precautions to prevent others from powering the system during repair/maintenance [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf, 006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

- Ensure residual energy is discharged and earth is correct: allow time for stored energy to discharge (30 s noted for power‑down) and check the earth/ground connection before re‑powering [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf, 015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Follow qualified procedures and documentation: conduct maintenance, inspection, calibration and repair according to the latest Service Manual; repair work should be done by Universal Robots or client‑designated trained individuals following the Service Manual [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Protect against electrical hazards: avoid disassembling the Control Box power supply too soon after switch‑off (high voltages up to ~600 V can be present for hours) and follow lockout/tagout and RCD/fuse/grounding requirements when working on mains [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf, 006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

- Observe ESD and contamination precautions: follow ESD regulations when disassembling components and prevent water/dust ingress to the robot arm or Control Box [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Verify safety functions after work: after maintenance/repair perform checks to ensure required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions, and adhere to applicable national/regional work‑safety regulations [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Use appropriate PPE and safe cleaning procedures: use recommended PPE (gloves, eye protection) for grease/cleaning work, do not use bleach, and do not use compressed air to clean the robot arm [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

If you need the specific step‑by‑step shutdown or inspection checklist, indicate which procedure and I will quote the exact steps from the manual.

QUESTION: How should the earth (ground) connection be checked after maintenance?
STUDENT ANSWER: Check the earth connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Verify the Protective Earth (PE) is connected to the M6-size screw terminals marked with earth symbols inside the Control Box. Ensure a solid mechanical and electrical connection. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Ensure the grounding conductor has at least the current rating of the highest current in the system and that all equipment shares a common grounding via the designated bolts. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Confirm all other power sources are off/locked out before re-energizing and that no external equipment can supply power to the robot during the check. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety-system state that applies an alternate (more restrictive) set of safety parameter values (e.g., joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed/force, momentum, power, stopping time/distance). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

When it is used:
- It is activated when the robot Tool or Elbow crosses a configured Trigger Reduced safety plane (the trigger starts at 20 mm around the plane and reduced limits take effect within that area), or when an external safety input causes the safety system to transition to Reduced mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Using an input to trigger Reduced mode can take up to 500 ms for the new limits to become active. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the four collaborative operation techniques defined in ISO 10218-1?
STUDENT ANSWER: The four collaborative operation techniques are: safety-rated monitored stop; hand-guiding; speed and separation monitoring (SSM); and power and force limiting (PFL). [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Supporting details:
- Safety-rated monitored stop: stop condition where position is held at a standstill and is monitored as a safety function.  
- Hand-guiding: individual/direct personal control while the robot is in automatic mode (UR robots provide hand-guided teach in manual mode, not for collaborative operation).  
- Speed and separation monitoring (SSM): maintaining a separation distance using Sensitive Protective Equipment (e.g., safety laser scanner) to enforce minimum protective distance and change safety function parameters or cause a monitored stop.  
- Power and force limiting (PFL): limiting energy transfer by robot design or control so contact will not cause injury; used to limit motion, speed, momentum, force, power, etc. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is an area or condition where body parts (e.g., fingers) can be caught between moving parts or between the robot and surrounding structures, potentially causing injury. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

Supporting points:
- The manual warns that handling tools/end effectors with sharp edges and/or pinch points can result in injury and to make sure tools have no sharp edges or pinch points; protective gloves/eyewear may be required. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Moving the robot in some axes when a tool is attached can present a pinch point—use caution when moving any axis. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Certain workspace areas are prone to pinching hazards (e.g., radial motions when wrist 1 is ≥450 mm from the base, and within 200 mm of the base when moving tangentially); these areas require special attention in the risk assessment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: Risk: Disturbing electromagnetic signals above the relevant IEC limits can cause unexpected robot behaviour and may permanently damage the robot; EMC problems are commonly seen in welding processes. Very strong magnetic fields can also damage the robot. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf] [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

How to avoid it:
- Ensure signal levels comply with applicable IEC EMC standards and avoid exposure to very high signal levels. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Keep I/O cable runs from the Control Box to other machinery ≤ 30 m unless additional EMC testing is performed. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf]
- Avoid placing the robot in strong magnetic fields and keep it away from welding or other high-EMC processes unless mitigations and testing are applied. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Reduced Mode is a state where the safety system uses the Reduced configuration limits for all safety functions (joint position/speed, TCP pose/speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time/distance, etc.). It is not itself a safety function, but a parametrization of safety limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf][019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- It can be initiated by a safety plane (Trigger Reduced Mode) or by an external safety input, and the system will apply reduced limits within about 500 ms when triggered by an input. When a plane triggers reduced mode, the transition includes a 20 mm transitional area around the trigger plane to prevent nuisance stops. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Normal and Reduced configurations are configurable safety parameter sets; you use Reduced Mode to adapt safety limits to different operating conditions or tool setups, validating appropriate values for your application per risk assessment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: High electromagnetic fields can cause malfunction; avoid long cables and maintain grounding.
STUDENT ANSWER: EMC interference risk: Very high signal levels or excessive exposure can permanently damage the robot, and EMC problems are often seen in welding processes (usually indicated by error messages in the log) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf].

 How to avoid it (from the same source):
 - Keep I/O interfacing and cables within EMC guidelines, and be aware that excessive signal levels can trigger issues.
 - Use only cables and interfaces as specified, and note that I/O cables from the Control Box to other equipment may have length limitations (not longer than 30 m) unless additional tests are performed. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Main safety precautions before maintenance:
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Check the earth connection before re-powering, observe ESD regulations, and prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Do not disassemble the power supply inside the Control Box or disassemble too quickly after switching off, as high voltages (up to 600 V) can be present for hours; follow all safety procedures in the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Reduced Mode is a state change of the safety system that parametrizes safety function limits (joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance). It is not itself a safety function. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf][019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- It can be activated by a safety plane/boundary or by an external input, and when active, all reduced-mode limits are active. The transition is designed to support ISO 13849-1 parametrization of safety functions. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf][019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- When triggered by a plane, there is a 20 mm area around the trigger plane where both normal and reduced limits are allowed to prevent nuisance stops; when triggered by an input, the new limits can take effect within up to 500 ms. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- Recovery and related behavior: Reduced Mode is a configuration used during risk-managed operation; if limits are violated, the safety system can stop per normal procedures, and recovery may be required. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf][019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can power the Control Box either from the internal 24V power supply (default) or from an external 24V supply by wiring the Power terminal block.

- Default (internal supply): use PWR (24V) and GND on the Power block. Internal 24V is typically 24 V (23–25 V) and provides up to 2 A (3.5 A for 500 ms or 33% duty cycle).  
- External supply (for more current): connect your external 24V to the lower terminals 24V and 0V on the Power block. External input must be 20–29 V and can supply up to 6 A.

Follow the Power terminal block wiring shown in the Control Box layout and observe the terminal labeling (PWR, GND, 24V, 0V). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

- Ensure safety function settings are set to the appropriate values determined by the robot application risk assessment. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

- Treat collaborative operation limits: collaborative applications are intended only for low‑risk situations; do not assume safe human interaction if the application or tooling increases risk. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

Note: Failure to follow these precautions can result in injury, death, or property damage. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

- CAUTION: placing the robot improperly can create pinch hazards that may lead to injury. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: Power the Control Box using the Power terminal block (the four Power terminals). By default the internal 24V supply is used: connect nothing to the lower 24V/0V terminals and use PWR (24V) and GND from the internal supply. If more current is needed, feed an external 24V supply to the lower two terminals (24V and 0V).

Electrical limits:
- Internal supply (PWR–GND): 23–25 V (typ 24 V), current 0–2 A (3.5 A for 500 ms or 33% duty cycle).  
- External 24V input (24V–0V): 20–29 V (typ 24 V), current up to 6 A.  

Configure the Power terminal block in the GUI if you change between internal and external supply. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed before first use or after any modification. Specifically:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) are functioning as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops; if safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Check the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the PolyScope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center (on) position must enable motion in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify a stop of the whole system. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test systems connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?

Supporting details:
- It affects joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- Reduced Mode can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starts at 2 cm from the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm) or by an input (reduced settings achieved within 500 ms). When the external connections are Low, Reduced Mode is initiated. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- It is a means of parametrization of safety functions in accordance with ISO 13849-1, and all parameter values must be verified and validated for the specific robot application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm, perform the commissioning checks described below to ensure safety and proper operation:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
- Test all connected safety inputs/outputs, including devices common to multiple machines/robots.
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if safeguard reset is configured, verify it functions as intended.
- Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
- Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope top-right corner.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify a system stop.
- Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify output changes are detected.
- Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

Source: [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Reduced Mode is a state change that activates all reduced safety-function limits (joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance). It is not a safety function itself. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- It can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starting within 2 cm of the plane) or by an input (reaching reduced settings within 500 ms). When external connections are Low, Reduced Mode is initiated. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- It is a means of parametrization of safety functions in accordance with ISO 13849-1; all parameter values need to be verified and validated for the specific application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: What is a pinch hazard in robot operation?
STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is a risk of injury from pinching injuries caused by the robot’s moving parts or nearby obstacles. You can avoid it by removing obstacles, placing the robot differently, or using safety planes and joint limits to prevent movement into pinch areas. Note that there are specific pinch zones: on the left for radial motions when the wrist 1 joint is at least 750 mm from the base, and on the right within 200 mm of the base when moving tangentially. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Use the Power block in the Control Box. The default is the internal 24V power supply (PWR to 24V and GND to 0V).
- If more current is needed, you can provide an external 24V supply to the same Power block (24V and 0V terminals) with 20–29 V and up to 6 A (3.5 A for 500 ms or 33% duty cycle).

Key terminals:
- Internal supply: PWR and GND (24V power for the I/O and systems).
- External supply option: 24V and 0V inputs on the Power block (external supply replaces internal for higher current). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm, run the Commissioning tests:
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
- Test all connected safety I/O, including devices common to multiple machines/robots.
- Test emergency stop buttons/inputs to ensure the robot stops and brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify motion stops; if safeguard reset is configured, check it functions.
- Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope top-right.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to ensure pressing to the center enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the E-Stop push-button and verify a system stop.
- Test outputs (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced/Not Reduced Mode) to verify the output changes are detected.
- Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

PolyScope screen.

motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: 1) Connect the Robot Cable between the robot arm and the Control Box and lock the connector (twist twice) before powering on. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

2) Plug the Control Box mains lead (IEC C13) into the IEC C14 inlet on the Control Box, using a country‑specific power cord (no adapters). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

3) Verify electrical protections and grounding are installed: connection to ground, main fuse, residual current device (RCD), and a lockable main switch (OFF position). Ensure all cables are correctly connected before power-up. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

4) Turn the robot on using the Teach Pendant power button (press to power on). Allow ~30 seconds after power‑off for discharge before servicing. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Warnings/notes:
- Do not extend or modify the original Robot Cable; do not use an adapter on the mains plug. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Ensure the Control Box has required clearance and is in an environment suited to its IP rating. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed for use “before using the robot application for the first time or after making any modifications.” [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Key checks (minimum):

- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops, and if safeguard reset is configured, confirm it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Verify initialization/reduced mode behaviour (observe initialization screen, activate reduced input and verify screen changes; change operational mode and verify mode icon changes). [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test the 3-position enabling device (center-on enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed). [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test outputs tied to system state (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, Not Reduced Mode) to verify output change detection. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Additional required actions from the application risk assessment:
- After physically installing/modifying the robot, verify connections, complete the integration, and determine appropriate safety configuration settings (password-protect safety configuration). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If any required test fails or hazards remain, follow the risk assessment process (ISO 12100 / ISO 10218-2 guidance) to specify additional safeguarding or configuration changes before returning the robot to service. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Read and follow the User Manual and all safety instructions before starting maintenance. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

- Perform an application risk assessment (responsibility of the integrator/user) that explicitly includes maintenance and troubleshooting tasks. Use ISO 12100 and ISO 10218-2 (and ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative cases) to identify hazards, severity, likelihood and avoidance. Do this before powering the robot after installation. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- Prevent unauthorized changes to safety settings by enabling password protection for the safety configuration; manage passwords so only qualified persons can change settings. Failure to set password protection can result in injury or death. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- Do not modify the robot or e‑series end caps; only authorized disassembly/reassembly at a UR service center or by skilled persons following the newest service manuals. Unauthorized modification can create unforeseen hazards. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

- Verify safety configuration settings that affect maintenance risks (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, joint/elbow/tool position limits, stopping time/distance limits). QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change that makes ALL reduced mode limits active, i.e., it changes the settings of safety function limits such as joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

When it is used / how it is initiated:
- It can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starts at 2 cm before the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm of the plane).  
- Or it can be initiated by an input (will achieve reduced settings within 500 ms) — when the configured external connections transition to Low, Reduced Mode is initiated.  
- Reduced Mode is a means of parametrization of safety functions in accordance with ISO 13849-1, and all parameter values must be verified and validated for the robot application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: 1) Make sure the installation and safety requirements are in place:
- Provide correct earth/ground connection, a main fuse, a Residual Current Device (RCD) and a lockable main switch (OFF position) for lockout.  
- Do not allow other equipment to supply power to the robot when locked out. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

2) Connect cables:
- Connect the Robot Cable between the robot arm and the Control Box and lock the connector. Do not extend or modify the Robot Cable. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]  
- Connect the IEC C13 power cord to the IEC C14 inlet on the Control Box. Use a country-specific wall plug on the power cord (do not use an adapter). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

3) Power source options for I/O (if applicable):
- If you need more I/O current, you can supply external 24V to the I/O power terminals instead of using the internal 24V supply. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

4) Apply mains power and switch on:
- With all connections and protective devices in place, plug the mains into the wall outlet and use the main switch to supply power to the Control Box. Then power the robot on from the Teach Pendant (use the Teach Pendant power button). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Warnings:
- Always ground the robot correctly and ensure input power is protected by the specified fuse and RCD.  
- Do not use adapters for the power cord. Do not disconnect the Robot Cable while the robot is powered. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must run the full commissioning checks listed for "before first use or after making any modifications" and also ensure the application risk assessment and safety configuration are updated.

Commissioning checks (perform all):  
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Inspect the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the Polyscope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center on position must enable motion in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the E‑stop push‑button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test any systems connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify their output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Determine and document the commissioning requirements specific to your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Risk assessment and safety configuration (must be done before powering on):  
- Conduct an application risk assessment per ISO 12100 and ISO 10218‑2 (integrator’s responsibility). Include tasks such as teaching, troubleshooting, maintenance, and normal operation. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Use the risk assessment to set appropriate safety configuration settings (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, joint/elbow/tool position and orientation limits, stopping time/distance limits). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]  
- Enable and set password protection for safety configuration to prevent unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If any required checks or risk‑mitigating measures cannot be completed or are inadequate, do not operate the robot until those issues are resolved. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Main answer:
Before maintenance, read and follow the User Manual, perform an application risk assessment that covers maintenance tasks, and do not modify the robot unless work is done by UR service personnel or skilled persons following the relevant service manual [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

- Prevent unauthorized changes by enabling password protection for safety configuration (manage passwords so only competent persons can change settings) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Do not modify the robot or e-Series end caps; authorized disassembling/reassembling shall be done at a UR service center or by skilled persons following the latest service manuals to avoid unforeseen hazards [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf].

GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.
STUDENT ANSWER: Submit to commissioning checks after any modification to the arm. Specifically, verify and test all safety inputs/outputs and related devices, test emergency stop and safeguard inputs, verify initialization/reduced input and mode icon, test the 3-position enabling device, test any Emergency Stop outputs and relevant system outputs, and determine the commissioning requirements for the application. QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Reduced Mode is a state change in which ALL reduced mode limits are ACTIVE, acting as a parametrization of safety function limits (e.g., joint position/speed, TCP pose/speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance) [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf].

- It can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starting at 2 cm from the plane; reduced mode settings are achieved within 2 cm) or by an input (achieving reduced settings within 500 ms). When external connections are Low, Reduced Mode is initiated [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf].

- Reduced Mode is not a safety function itself; it is a state used to configure safety function limits according to ISO 13849-1, and all parameter values must be verified for the specific application [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf].

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm, run the commissioning checks listed in the commissioning document.

Key checks:
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots).
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to ensure the robot stops and brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops; verify functionality of safeguard reset if configured.
- Look at the initialization screen, activate reduced input, and verify the screen changes.
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope top-right.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to confirm that pressing to the center enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify a system stop.
- Test systems connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify output changes are detected.
- Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

Source: 009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

It is not a safety function itself; it parametrizes safety-function limits (joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance) to suit the application, per ISO 13849-1. QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: 1) Connect the mains power cord: plug the supplied IEC C13 end into the Control Box IEC C14 inlet, and fit a country‑specific wall plug on the other end. Ensure the installation includes a ground connection, correct mains fuse, a Residual Current Device (RCD) and a lockable (OFF) main switch [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

2) Connect robot and I/O cables first: connect and lock the Robot Cable/Base Flange Cable and any external cables (do not extend or modify the Robot Cable) before powering the Control Box [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

3) Ensure the Teach Pendant is powered off and connected before powering the Control Box: do not connect or disconnect the Teach Pendant while the Control Box is powered on [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf].

4) Power on: after all connections and grounding are verified, plug the mains into the wall outlet and use the Teach Pendant power button to turn the robot on (the Assembly section instructs to “Plug in the mains” and the Teach Pendant power button is used to turn the robot on/off) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

Safety reminders: always ensure correct grounding, RCD and fuse protection, keep the Control Box in an environment suited to its IP rating, and allow required clearances for cooling [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed below after any modification, and you must perform an application risk assessment for the modified robot application.

Commissioning tests (perform all): [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.  
- Test that all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) function as intended.  
- Test emergency stop buttons/inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, verify it functions as intended.  
- Check the initialization screen, activate the reduced mode input and verify the screen changes.  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of PolyScope.  
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center position must enable motion in manual mode at reduced speed.  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops.  
- Test system responses to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, and Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify output changes are detected.  
- Determine and document any additional commissioning requirements specific to your robot application.

Risk assessment requirement (perform/confirm): [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Conduct an application risk assessment (integrator’s responsibility) before powering on after modification; use ISO 12100 and ISO 10218-2 (and ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative applications) to identify required safety configuration settings and additional protective measures.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: - Read and follow the User Manual and the recommendations for intended use before doing maintenance [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf].

- Prevent unauthorized changes to safety settings by enabling password protection and manage passwords so only qualified persons can change configuration [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

- Do not modify the robot or e-Series end caps; any authorized disassembly/reassembly must be done at a UR service center or per the applicable service manual by skilled persons [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf].

- When lifting or moving the robot or Control Box during maintenance, use correct lifting techniques and equipment, follow regional/national lifting guidelines, hold both tubes of the arm when moving it, and make sure base mounting bolts are securely tightened before release [014__L1__14._Transportation__pp190-191.pdf].

Note: Specific lock-out/tag-out, electrical isolation, or step-by-step maintenance procedures are not provided in the supplied documents.

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change that applies the robot’s "reduced" safety parameter set (i.e., lower limits for joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed/force, momentum, power, stopping time and stopping distance) — it is not itself a safety function. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

When it is used:
- It is initiated automatically by a Trigger Reduced Plane/boundary (starts at 2 cm from the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm of the plane). [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- Or it can be activated by a safety input (external connections low), in which case the robot adapts to the reduced limits within up to 500 ms. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]  
- The Reduced/Normal parameter sets and their transition behavior (including a 20 mm buffer zone around a trigger plane to avoid nuisance stops) are configurable in the safety parameter set. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the four collaborative operation techniques defined in ISO 10218-1?
STUDENT ANSWER: The four collaborative operation techniques are: safety-rated monitored stop; hand-guiding; speed and separation monitoring (SSM) safety functions; and power and force limiting (PFL) by inherent design or control. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Brief explanations (from the source):
- Safety-rated monitored stop: position held at standstill and monitored as a safety function (UR safeguard stop is a safety-rated monitored stop).  
- Hand-guiding: individual/direct personal control while in automatic mode; UR provides freedrive for programming in manual mode, not hand-guiding in automatic mode.  
- Speed and separation monitoring (SSM): maintains a separation distance using sensitive protective equipment (e.g., safety laser scanner) to switch safety parameters or invoke a monitored stop.  
- Power and force limiting (PFL): robot design/control limits energy transfer to a person; UR robots are PFL-capable to limit motion, speed, momentum, force and power. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]
